title: Time Toxicity and End-of-Life Treatment of Metastatic Pancreatic Cancer.
abstract: Optimal care for patients with metastatic pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) requires coordination across multiple providers, creating substantial time toxicity-the time patients spend engaged with the health care system. This study quantified total time toxicity and identified predictors of prolonged time toxicity in patients with metastatic PDAC. We retrospectively analyzed patients with metastatic PDAC treated at a high-volume center from 2018 to 2022, excluding those who did not receive cancer-directed therapy or received care at multiple facilities. Time toxicity was defined as the proportion of overall survival (OS) spent in cancer-related health care encounters, with hospice time excluded. Beta regression identified predictors of time toxicity, incorporating OS as a scaling factor. Secondary outcomes included systemic therapy in the last 30 days of life, hospice transition after hospitalization, and inpatient death. Among 177 patients (median age 66 years; 57.1% male; 81.9% White), the majority received chemotherapy (n = 175) and palliative care consultation (n = 107). Median total time toxicity was 20% (IQR, 15%-28%), including 7% inpatient (IQR, 3%-16%) and 10% ambulatory (IQR, 8%-13%). Overall, 39% (n = 69) received systemic therapy in the last 30 days of life, 42.4% (n = 75) transitioned to hospice after hospitalization, and 14.8% (n = 21) died inpatient. On multivariable analysis, older age, rural/urban residence, and chemotherapy regimen predicted time toxicity (all P < .05). Each additional year of age was associated with a reduced time toxicity of 0.29%; urban residence was associated with a 3.3% increase in time toxicity compared with rural; and receiving multiple chemotherapy regimens was associated with 8.65% decrease compared with 5-fluorouracil-based regimens only. Patients with metastatic PDAC spend roughly 1 in 5 days of survival engaged in health care interactions. Demographic, socioeconomic, and treatment-related factors all influence time toxicity.

title: Genomic Landscape of Gastroenteropancreatic Neuroendocrine Neoplasms Using Panel Sequencing.
abstract: The clinical utility of genomic profiling in gastroenteropancreatic neuroendocrine neoplasms (GEP-NENs) remains incompletely defined, particularly for clinically relevant annotated alterations and prognostic stratification. We performed a multi-institutional analysis to characterize genomic alterations across GEP-NEN subtypes, generate prevalence estimates to inform precision oncology efforts, and evaluate associations with clinical actionability and survival. We performed a retrospective analysis of 1,691 GEP-NENs from the American Association for Cancer Research Project Genomics Evidence Neoplasia Information Exchange database. Tumors were classified into neuroendocrine tumors (NETs) or neuroendocrine carcinomas (NECs) and stratified by primary site. Genomic alterations, including single-nucleotide variants, insertions/deletions, copy number alterations, and structural variants, were analyzed using a panel-adjusted approach. Alterations were annotated for clinical relevance using multiple knowledge bases. Overall survival was evaluated in a subset (n = 502) with available data. Genomic alterations were identified in 86.5% of patients. NETs were enriched for alterations in chromatin-remodeling genes (MEN1, DAXX) and mTOR pathway regulator TSC2, whereas NECs were characterized by canonical drivers (TP53, RB1, KRAS, APC, and BRAF). Annotated alterations were identified in 34.1% of all patients, with higher rates in NECs compared with NETs (74.4% v 28.5%, P < .001). Notable annotated targets included BRAF V600E (2.2%; 14.8% of all colorectal NECs), KRAS-activating mutations (6.8%; 0.35% G12C), and NTRK fusions (0.2%). Annotation rates varied by primary site with the highest rates observed in colorectal, gastric, and esophageal NECs. In NETs, the presence of NEC-associated driver alterations was associated with worse overall survival (hazard ratio, 3.67 [95% CI, 2.49 to 5.42], P < .001). Genomic profiling reveals meaningful differences in biomarker prevalence and prognosis across GEP-NEN subtypes. These findings support integrating genomic profiling with histologic classification to refine risk stratification and inform biomarker-driven clinical trials.

title: Role of Substance P in physiological and pathological states of the pancreas.
abstract: Background Substance P (SP), a neuropeptide acting mainly through its high-affinity neurokinin-1 receptor (NK-1R), is a key signaling molecule in the pancreas. It is integral to the neuro-pancreatic axis, but its role shifts dramatically between physiological and pathological states. Summary Acting through NK-1R, SP plays various roles in the pancreatic physiological state and disease state. Under physiological conditions, SP contributes to the regulation of exocrine and endocrine functions. In pathological settings, SP signaling exerts effects on modulation of immunity, β-cell preservation and insulin sensitivity in diabetes, triggers neurogenic inflammation and chronic pain in pancreatitis, and enhances malignant behaviours and perineural invasion in pancreatic cancer. Key Messages Functioning as an important regulator, SP maintains physiological balance in health yet drives disease progression in diabetes, pancreatitis, and pancreatic cancer. The SP/NK-1R axis has therapeutic potential with its beneficial actions.

title: Imaging classification of pancreatic cystic lesions: a radiologist's guide.
abstract: Pancreatic cystic lesions (PCLs) are increasingly encountered in clinical practice owing to the widespread use of high-resolution cross-sectional imaging. These lesions comprise a heterogeneous group of entities ranging from benign cysts to pre-malignant neoplasms and invasive cancers, making accurate characterization essential for appropriate patient surveillance and therapeutic management. Imaging plays a pivotal role in lesion detection, differential diagnosis, and assessment of malignant potential. This review presents a practical imaging-based classification of PCLs founded on lesion morphology, relationship to the pancreatic ductal system, enhancement patterns, and associated imaging features. Using a stepwise diagnostic approach, pancreatic cystic lesions are categorized according to their increasing risk of malignancy into non-neoplastic cysts, serous cystic neoplasms, mucinous cystic lesions, and cystic degeneration of solid pancreatic tumors. Characteristic imaging findings, relevant differential diagnostic considerations, and imaging features associated with increased malignant potential are comprehensively reviewed, with particular emphasis on the role of MRI and MR cholangiopancreatography (MRCP) in lesion characterization. A structured pattern-recognition flowchart is proposed to facilitate routine image interpretation and enhance diagnostic confidence. In addition, a practical reporting template is presented to promote standardized assessment and effective communication within multidisciplinary teams. Emerging techniques, including diffusion-weighted imaging, quantitative MRI biomarkers, radiomics, artificial intelligence, and molecular analysis of cyst fluid, are discussed as promising tools for improving diagnostic accuracy and refining risk stratification. By emphasizing readily recognizable imaging features and a systematic diagnostic workflow, this review provides radiologists with a practical and clinically applicable framework for the evaluation, diagnosis, risk assessment, and multidisciplinary management of pancreatic cystic lesions.

title: GLP-1 RA Prescribing in Patients With Type 2 Diabetes and Cancer.
abstract: Glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1 RAs) are increasingly used to treat type 2 diabetes, yet little is known about its utilization patterns in patients with cancer history, given limited oncology-specific guidance. To evaluate trends and factors associated with GLP-1 RA use among Medicare beneficiaries with type 2 diabetes, comparing those with and without cancer history. This retrospective cohort study used Surveillance, Epidemiology, and End Results-Medicare linked data to identify patients diagnosed with 7 common cancers in 2010 to 2021 and preexisting type 2 diabetes before cancer diagnosis. A noncancer cohort with type 2 diabetes was identified from a 5% random sample of Medicare beneficiaries and matched 1:1 to patients with cancer based on sociodemographic characteristics; controls were assigned a pseudo-index date corresponding to their matched patient's cancer diagnosis date. Beneficiaries were followed up annually until death or December 31, 2022, for TM or December 31, 2021, for MA. Data were analyzed from December 2025 to July 2026. Diagnosis of 1 of 7 common cancers. Any GLP-1 RA use. Proportions of beneficiaries with any GLP-1 RA use annually were stratified by traditional Medicare (TM) and Medicare Advantage (MA). Multivariable logistic regression examined (1) differences in GLP-1RA use between cancer and noncancer cohorts with and without adjusting for sociodemographic characteristics and comorbidities and diabetes-related complications; (2) cancer-specific factors associated with GLP-1RA use among the cancer cohort after 2018. A total of 373 278 Medicare beneficiaries (mean [SD] age, 76.1 [6.6] years; 188 746 [50.6%] female) with cancer and diabetes and 373 278 noncancer controls (153 358 unique beneficiaries) were included. GLP-1 RA use increased from 85 beneficiaries (0.5%) to 9083 beneficiaries (8.2%) and from 138 beneficiaries (0.9%) to 9300 beneficiaries (6.2%) in the cancer and noncancer cohorts, respectively, from 2010 to 2022 under TM; a similar increase was observed under MA. Despite higher unadjusted GLP-1 RA use among the cancer cohort than the noncancer cohort (probability difference, TM: 1.19 [95% CI, 0.94 to 1.44] percentage points [pp]; P < .001; MA: 0.45 [95% CI, 0.21 to 0.68] pp, P < .001), adjusted analysis showed no significant differences in GLP-1 RA use under TM (adjusted probability difference, 0.16 [95% CI, -0.10 to 0.41,] pp; P = .22) and lower use among cancer cohort under MA (-0.52 [95% CI, -0.76 to -0.28] pp; P < .001). Complications or comorbidities, including obesity (adjusted probability difference, TM: 3.35 [95% CI, 3.10 to 3.61] pp; P < .001; MA: 2.42 [95% CI, 2.19 to 2.64] pp; P < .001), dyslipidemia (adjusted probability difference, TM: 2.26 [95% CI, 2.03 to 2.50] pp; P < .001; MA: 1.80 [95% CI, 1.57 to 2.03] pp; P < .001), neuropathy (adjusted probability difference: TM: 3.91 [95% CI, 3.64 to 4.19] pp; P < .001; MA: 3.17 [95% CI, 2.94 to 3.41] pp; P < .001), retinopathy (adjusted probability difference, TM: 2.02 [95% CI, 1.78 to 2.27] pp; P < .001; MA: 1.84 [95% CI, 1.63 to 2.06] pp; P < .001), and chronic kidney disease (adjusted probability difference, TM: 2.01 [95% CI, 1.76 to 2.26] pp; P < .001; MA: 1.63 [95% CI, 1.40 to 1.85] pp; P < .001) were associated with greater likelihood of GLP-1RA use. Within the cancer cohort, breast (adjusted probability difference, TM: 1.05 [95% CI, 0.43 to 1.66] pp; P = .001; MA: 0.89 [95% CI, 0.37 to 1.41] pp; P = .001), gynecologic (adjusted probability difference, MA: 1.13 [95% CI, 0.45 to 1.81] pp; P = .001), and prostate (adjusted probability difference, TM: 1.30 [95% CI, 0.72 to 1.88] pp; P < .001; MA: 1.07 [95% CI, 0.56 to 1.58] pp; P < .001) cancers were associated with higher GLP-1 RA use than colorectal cancer, while pancreatic cancer was associated with lower GLP-1 RA use (adjusted probability difference, TM: -2.55 [95% CI, -3.17 to -1.93] pp; P < .001; MA: -1.64 [95% CI, -2.23 to -1.05] pp; P < .001). In this retrospective study of Medicare beneficiaries with type 2 diabetes, GLP-1 RA use increased substantially and primarily was associated with metabolic risk profile, with limited associations with cancer status. Variation across cancer types and stages suggests oncologic context may influence prescribing.

title: International expert consensus on perioperative management of carcinoid crisis.
abstract: Carcinoid crisis is a critical concern for patients with neuroendocrine tumours undergoing invasive procedures. Guidance is needed to standardize and optimize perioperative care for patients at risk of carcinoid crisis. Consensus-based expert recommendations were developed for the perioperative management of carcinoid crisis among patients with midgut and bronchopulmonary neuroendocrine tumours undergoing non-cardiac surgery. A modified Delphi approach was used with four rounds of voting to reach expert consensus on statements about perioperative management of carcinoid crisis. A multidisciplinary international panel of 44 experts was formed, and 3 patient partners were engaged. Statements addressing preoperative, intraoperative, and postoperative considerations were created. Panellists rated statements on a Likert scale (from 1 to 7). Three additional rounds of iterative rating and feedback were completed anonymously. Consensus was defined with median score between 5 and 7, and ≤ 13 panellists rating outside the score category containing the median. Final consensus was reached on 41 statements. Of these, 12 focused on preoperative work-up and optimization, 27 on intraoperative management including monitoring, prophylaxis, and treatment of crisis, and 2 on postoperative management. The principal practice-shifting recommendations were that somatostatin analogues are not necessary for prophylaxis before surgery or on the day of operation, and treatment in the event of carcinoid crisis should start with vasopressors, with short-acting somatostatin analogues used as an adjunct. Using modified Delphi methodology, recommendations to guide the perioperative management of carcinoid crisis were developed. Considering the importance of carcinoid crisis on the management and outcomes of patients undergoing surgical resection for neuroendocrine tumours, this guidance can help standardize care and optimize outcomes.

title: Characterizing bone metastases and skeletal-related events in patients with well-differentiated neuroendocrine neoplasms utilizing <sup>68</sup>Gallium-DOTATATE positron emission tomography.
abstract: Tumors of neuroendocrine origin are a heterogenous group of related neoplasms which can arise from anywhere in the body. Neuroendocrine neoplasms (NENs) are categorized by site of origin, differentiation status and grade (Ki-67 expression and/or mitotic rate), with significant prognostic variability accordingly. Historically, the prevalence of bone metastasis is reported to be 6%-12% based on "first generation" (i.e., <sup>111</sup>Indium pentetreotide [Octreoscan®]) somatostatin receptor imaging (SSRI). We conducted a retrospective cohort study including patients with well-differentiated NENs to determine the clinical and imaging characteristics of osseous metastases when evaluated with higher-sensitivity <sup>68</sup>Gallium-DOTATATE positron emission tomography (PET) scans, as well as determining fracture prevalence in selected sub-cohorts. We also developed a risk score analysis to assess risk of fracture in this cohort. Four hundred twenty-four patients were identified for inclusion. The median age was 61 years. Most patients were asymptomatic (64%), had sclerotic lesions (77%), Krenning 4 (71%), and had >3 sites (69%) of osseous disease. A high proportion of patients had osseous metastases at sites with high risk for fracture, including vertebra (82%), pelvis (63%), and peri-trochanteric femur (34%). Fifty-seven patients (13%) in the entire cohort suffered a fracture. Fracture prevalence was significantly lower in small bowel neuroendocrine tumors (NETs, 7%) and Grades 1 and 2 disease (8% and 9%, respectively), with higher prevalence in pancreatic NETs, paragangliomas/pheochromocytomas, lung carcinoid, and Grade 3 disease (≥20% for each; p-values <.05). Our study showed that the rate of osseous metastatic disease approximates 20% in well-differentiated NENs. Most bone metastases are asymptomatic and the risk of fracture is variable based on the primary site of disease and tumor grade. Our novel risk score analysis for fracture was designed to assist clinician decision making as to management of bone metastasis in this patient population.

title: The Gut Virome in Gastrointestinal Cancers: Mechanisms, Biomarkers, and Translational Opportunities.
abstract: The gastrointestinal tract contains a dense multi-kingdom ecosystem in which bacteria, fungi, archaea, viruses, the mucosa, and the immune system interact. Although cancer microbiome research has focused mainly on bacteria, the gut virome dominated by bacteriophages may influence gastrointestinal carcinogenesis by reshaping bacterial communities, transferring functional genes, modulating inflammation, and altering treatment response. The strongest evidence comes from colorectal cancer, where multiple cohorts show altered phage diversity, temperate-phage enrichment, disrupted phage-bacteria networks, and reproducible stool-based diagnostic signals. Emerging studies in pancreatic cancer, esophageal adenocarcinoma, hepatocellular carcinoma, and precursor lesions suggest that virome disruption extends beyond colorectal cancer, although evidence remains uneven. Classic oncogenic viruses, including Epstein-Barr virus and hepatitis viruses, provide complementary examples of direct viral carcinogenesis in digestive organs. Anelloviruses are widespread in healthy individuals and are not established causes of cancer, but their abundance and composition may reflect immune status, inflammation, tissue injury, and altered host viral ecology. Virome-related interventions remain clinically immature: fecal microbiota transplantation has reached small phase I/II studies in gastrointestinal cancers, whereas phage, fecal-filtrate, and fecal virome approaches remain preclinical or non-oncology; direct oncolytic viruses have reached late-phase testing. Major barriers include viral dark matter, specimen and assay heterogeneity, disease-related confounding, limited external validation, and weak causal evidence. Standardized, mechanistically anchored, multi-kingdom studies are needed to establish clinical utility.

title: Long-Term Drug Screening Identifies PARP Inhibitors as Irinotecan Combination Partners in BRCA1/2-Wild-Type Pancreatic Ductal Adenocarcinoma.
abstract: Background/Objectives: Irinotecan is a component of standard first-line regimens for advanced pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC), yet cells that survive irinotecan treatment may retain the capacity to re-establish growth. Most anticancer drug screens use short-term growth inhibition as an initial criterion for compound selection, potentially excluding compounds with limited acute activity. We asked whether some of these excluded candidates might nevertheless show substantial long-term activity and enhance irinotecan responses in combination. Methods: We first screened 3524 compounds for short-term growth inhibition and advanced compounds with limited acute activity to a 10-day colony-growth screen. Long-term hits were narrowed to clinically relevant anticancer agents and then screened with irinotecan. Talazoparib showed the lowest combination-to-single-agent score and was selected for further evaluation. The combination was evaluated across multiple BRCA1/2-wild-type PDAC cell lines and further validated using additional PARP inhibitors and a xenograft model. RNA sequencing and γH2AX analysis were used to examine associated DNA damage-response features. Results: Of the 1877 compounds advanced from the initial 3-day screen, 334 (17.8%) met the long-term hit criterion. In short- versus long-term comparisons, irinotecan plus talazoparib produced greater growth suppression and higher Bliss synergy scores in 10-day than in 72 h assays. Enhanced long-term responses were observed across five BRCA1/2-wild-type PDAC cell lines, and similar long-term effects were observed with three additional PARP inhibitors. The combination also showed synergistic antitumor activity in an MIA PaCa-2 subcutaneous xenograft model. Transcriptomic and γH2AX analyses provided findings consistent with replication-stress and DNA-damage-response processes. Conclusions: A substantial subset of compounds with limited acute activity showed substantial long-term activity. PARP inhibition enhanced irinotecan responses and emerged as a candidate combination strategy in BRCA1/2-wild-type PDAC.

title: Development of a GRPR-Targeted <sup>99m</sup>Tc/<sup>188</sup>Re Theranostic Pair Based on NOTA-P2-RM26.
abstract: Background: Gastrin-releasing peptide receptor (GRPR)-targeted radioligands are promising tools for imaging and treatment of GRPR-expressing malignancies. This study aimed to develop a NOTA-P2-RM26-based 99mTc/188Re theranostic pair using the fac-[M(CO)3]+ core, with fac-[99mTc][Tc(CO)3(NOTA-P2-RM26)], 99mTc2, as the diagnostic SPECT analogue and fac-[188Re][Re(CO)3(NOTA-P2-RM26)], 188Re2, as the potential therapeutic counterpart. Methods: NOTA-P2-RM26 was radiolabeled with the fac-[99mTc(CO)3(H2O)3]+, 99mTc1, precursor after systematic optimization of peptide amount, pH, buffer, temperature, and reaction time. The radioconjugate was purified by HPLC, reformulated by solid-phase extraction, and evaluated by radio-HPLC and radio-TLC. We assessed stability in the formulation, human serum, cysteine and histidine over 6 h. Lipophilicity was determined as logD7.4. We evaluated in vitro specificity, cell association, and internalization in PC-3 cells. We performed biodistribution, blocking, dynamic imaging, and SPECT/CT imaging in PC-3 xenograft-bearing mice. The corresponding 188Re analog was prepared under analogous conditions and evaluated for physicochemical matching. Results: Optimized labeling afforded 99mTc2 with approximately 85% radiochemical conversion and >97% radiochemical purity after purification. The compound remained stable in formulation, with 93% of the tracer intact after 6 h, and exhibited a hydrophilic profile (logD7.4 = -1.5 ± 0.2). In PC-3 cells, uptake reached 20.0 ± 1.0% of added activity and was reduced to 1.4 ± 0.3% under blocking conditions. In vivo, tumor uptake was 15.0 ± 1.0 %IA/g at 30 min and 17.0 ± 2.2 %IA/g at 1 h p.i. Blocking reduced tumor uptake to 0.84 ± 0.12 %IA/g, corresponding to approximately 95% inhibition. Pancreatic uptake decreased from 8.0 ± 0.4 %IA/g at 30 min to 3.0 ± 0.35 %IA/g at 1 h and was reduced to 0.20 ± 0.08 %IA/g after blocking. At 1 h p.i., tumor-to-blood, tumor-to-muscle, tumor-to-pancreas, and tumor-to-kidney ratios were approximately 21.3, 130.8, 5.7, and 3.6, respectively. SPECT/CT imaging confirmed clear, blockable visualization of the PC-3 tumor. The 188Re analog was obtained with approximately 80% radiochemical conversion and >95% radiochemical purity post purification. It showed similar stability values to 99mTc2 under the tested conditions and a logD7.4 of -1.6 ± 0.2. Conclusions: Complex 99mTc2 demonstrated efficient preparation, high stability, GRPR-mediated tumor uptake, favorable tumor-to-background ratios, and clear SPECT/CT visualization of PC-3 xenografts. The corresponding 188Re analog supports the feasibility of a chemically matched 99mTc/188Re NOTA-P2-RM26 theranostic platform and warrants further evaluation of 188Re biodistribution, dosimetry, and therapeutic efficacy.

title: CCKBR (Gastrin Receptor) as a Theranostic Target in Oncology: Biological Rationale, Diagnostic Imaging, and Next-Generation Peptide-Based Drug Development.
abstract: Cholecystokinin B receptor (CCKBR) is a promising theranostic target because of its overexpression in several malignancies, including medullary thyroid carcinoma, small-cell lung cancer, gastric cancer, and pancreatic cancer. Its high-affinity ligand binding and efficient receptor-mediated internalization provide a strong biological basis for molecular imaging and peptide receptor radionuclide therapy (PRRT). Recent advances in radiolabeled gastrin and mini-gastrin analogues have improved tumor targeting, metabolic stability, and pharmacokinetic profiles, supporting their application in both diagnostic imaging and radionuclide therapy. This review summarizes the molecular biology and tumor expression of CCKBR, recent progress in SPECT/PET imaging and targeted radionuclide therapy, and advances in ligand and pharmacokinetic engineering. Despite substantial progress, CCKBR-targeted theranostics remain less clinically established than SSTR- or PSMA-based platforms. Major challenges include heterogeneous receptor expression, renal and gastric uptake, limited prospective clinical evidence, and the lack of standardized imaging, dosimetry, and treatment protocols. Addressing these limitations will be essential for the broader clinical translation of CCKBR-targeted theranostics.

title: Bremachlorin-Based Photodynamic-Therapy-Induced Effects in Low-Oxygenated Pancreatic Ductal Adenocarcinoma (PDAC) Tumor Microenvironment.
abstract: Photodynamic therapy (PDT) is a minimally invasive treatment whose efficacy is strongly influenced by tumor oxygenation and the tumor microenvironment (TME). Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) is characterized by severe hypoxia, dense stroma, and immune suppression, limiting therapeutic responsiveness. In this study, we investigated how Bremachlorin-based PDT remodels the TME in two murine PDAC models with distinct immune phenotypes (T-cell-high and T-cell-low) and compared them with the immunogenic MC38 colon carcinoma model. Single-fiber reflectance and fluorescence spectroscopy were used to monitor tumor physiology and photosensitizer dynamics during PDT, while multiplex immunohistochemistry enabled spatial profiling of stromal and immune components post-treatment. PDAC tumors exhibited significantly lower baseline oxygenation than MC38 tumors, which was not substantially improved by reducing the PDT fluence rate from 116 to 50 mW·cm<sup>-2</sup>. Nevertheless, PDT reduced collagen type I content in both PDAC models, indicating stromal remodeling. Importantly, illumination with a moderate fluence rate of 50 mW·cm<sup>-2</sup> significantly increased CD8<sup>+</sup> T-cell infiltration and improved the CD8<sup>+</sup>/neutrophil ratio in T-cell-high PDAC tumors, suggesting a shift toward a less immunosuppressive immune landscape. These findings demonstrate that Bremachlorin-PDT can modulate the PDAC tumor microenvironment and highlight the importance of immune context in shaping PDT outcomes, supporting rational optimization of PDT-based combination therapies.

title: CGRP-RAMP1/CALCRL Signaling Drives TGF-β2-Mediated Immune Evasion and Pancreatic Cancer Progression.
abstract: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) is characterized by extensive neural remodeling and a profoundly immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment, both of which contribute to disease progression and therapeutic resistance. However, whether nociceptor-derived signals directly reprogram PDAC cells to promote immune evasion remains poorly understood. Here, we identify a previously unrecognized tumor-intrinsic neuroimmune mechanism driven by calcitonin gene-related peptide (CGRP) signaling through the receptor complex RAMP1/CALCRL on PDAC cells. CRISPR/Cas9-mediated deletion of Ramp1 or Calcrl did not alter PDAC cell proliferation in vitro but markedly suppressed tumor growth and prolonged survival in immunocompetent mice. These antitumor effects were lost in immunodeficient hosts, indicating that the pro-tumorigenic function of CGRP signaling depends on an intact host immune system. Consistently, tumor cell-specific loss of Ramp1 or Calcrl remodeled the tumor immune microenvironment, enhancing CD4+ and CD8+ T-cell effector activity. Mechanistically, CGRP stimulation promoted TGF-β2 expression and secretion by PDAC cells in a RAMP1-dependent manner. Tumor-derived TGF-β2 subsequently acted in a paracrine fashion to suppress CD8+ T-cell activation and cytotoxic function, whereas genetic disruption of RAMP1 or pharmacological inhibition of TGF-β signaling relieved this immunosuppression. Together, these findings define a CGRP-RAMP1/CALCRL-TGF-β2 signaling axis through which nociceptive input is converted into tumor-driven adaptive immune evasion in PDAC. This pathway reveals a previously underappreciated mechanism linking neural signaling to PDAC progression and identifies CGRP receptor signaling as a potential therapeutic vulnerability for restoring antitumor immunity and improving the responsiveness of PDAC to immunotherapy.

title: An Overview of Cushing's Syndrome Caused by Ectopic Adrenocorticotropin Secretion.
abstract: Ectopic Cushing's syndrome (ECS) causes 10% to 20% of all cases of endogenous hypercortisolism. It is caused by the aberrant secretion of adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH) or corticotropin-releasing hormone (CRH) due to the presence of an ectopic tumor. The latter is usually a neuroendocrine (NEN) tumor (mostly thoracic NENs such as bronchial NEN neoplasms, thymic NEN neoplasms, small cell lung carcinoma (SCLC), or pancreatic NEN neoplasms). Clinical presentation is heterogeneous: an aggressive phenotype, typically driven by rapidly growing, poorly differentiated tumors such as small-cell lung carcinoma, manifests with severe symptoms of acute onset, predominant myopathy, resistant arterial hypertension, hypokalemia, and severe hyperpigmentation, usually without the centripetal obesity typical of Cushing's syndrome; conversely, an indolent phenotype, more often related to well-differentiated neuroendocrine neoplasms such as bronchial carcinoids, may present with the classic centripetal fat distribution, facial plethora, and purple striae also seen in Cushing's disease, making clinical distinction between the two difficult. The diagnosis of ECS can be cumbersome and time-consuming. Once hypercortisolism is confirmed, the most critical step is to distinguish patients with an ectopic source of ACTH from those with pituitary adenoma. Dynamic endocrine tests such as the high-dose dexamethasone suppression test, CRH stimulation tests, desmopressin tests, and bilateral inferior petrosal sinus sampling (BIPSS) can be helpful in the differential diagnosis. BIPSS is considered the gold standard for distinguishing a pituitary from a non-pituitary source of ACTH: the absence of a central-to-peripheral ACTH gradient supports, but does not by itself localize or confirm, an ectopic source. Tumor localization is achieved by a multimodality imaging protocol, including initial high-resolution computed tomography (CT) scans, followed by functional imaging, mainly Gallium-68-labeled somatostatin receptor positron emission tomography (PET)/CT scans. However, in 10-20% of these patients, the tumors cannot be localized. The treatment of ACTH-dependent hypercortisolism is two-fold: one is to immediately control hypercortisolism to prevent life-threatening complications (opportunistic infections and thromboembolism), and the second is to definitively treat the tumor. Medical treatment with steroidogenesis inhibitors, including metyrapone, ketoconazole, and osilodrostat, or surgical management (bilateral adrenalectomy) can be effective in immediately controlling hypercortisolism. Definitive surgical resection of the tumor is the hoped-for final treatment. The prognosis is variable, depending on the nature of the underlying neoplasm, ranging from excellent in patients with resected bronchial carcinoids to dismal in those with SCLC.

title: Staged Surgery for Synchronous Proximal Gastric Adenocarcinoma and Pancreatic Head Ductal Adenocarcinoma with an Early Favorable Outcome: A Case Report.
abstract: Background. Synchronous primary gastric cancer and pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) are uncommon, and published experience with their combined treatment is limited. Proximal gastric adenocarcinoma combined with pancreatic head PDAC presents a particular challenge because resection and reconstruction must address two anatomically separate primary tumors. Materials and Methods. A 62-year-old man with poorly differentiated proximal gastric adenocarcinoma (cT3N0M0) and pancreatic head PDAC (cT3N1M0) received six cycles of neoadjuvant FOLFIRINOX. Preoperative ECOG performance status was 0. Treatment comprised proximal gastrectomy with D2 lymphadenectomy and double-tract reconstruction and, approximately 10 weeks later, pylorus-preserving pancreatoduodenectomy. Contrast-enhanced CT before the second stage showed no disease progression. Results. Intra-abdominal hemorrhage after proximal gastrectomy required relaparotomy. Histopathological examination confirmed microscopically negative resection margins (R0) for both tumors. Gastric tumor regression was Becker grade 3, indicating minimal or no regression; pancreatic regression was Modified Ryan score 3, indicating a poor or absent response. Six cycles of adjuvant modified FOLFIRINOX were reported. At the last reported follow-up, 10 months after the second operation, the patient had no evidence of progression and an ECOG performance status of 0. Conclusions. This case documents the technical feasibility of staged gastric and pancreatic resection after neoadjuvant chemotherapy in a patient with preoperative ECOG performance status 0, with histologically negative resection margins and an early favorable outcome despite a postoperative complication. The reported R0 status describes the morphological assessment of resection margins. Longer follow-up is required to assess durable disease control.

title: PG-SGA, GLIM, and CONUT in Hepatopancreatobiliary Cancer: Complementary Tools for Different Clinical Questions.
abstract: Malnutrition is among the most consequential yet inconsistently addressed comorbidities in hepatopancreatobiliary (HPB) cancer, arising at the intersection of cachexia, sarcopenia, systemic inflammation, hepatic dysfunction, and biliary obstruction. The Patient-Generated Subjective Global Assessment (PG-SGA), the Global Leadership Initiative on Malnutrition (GLIM) framework, and the Controlling Nutritional Status (CONUT) score are often used interchangeably, but they serve different purposes: nutritional assessment, malnutrition diagnosis, and prognostic risk stratification, respectively. This narrative review compares what the three tools measure, summarizes the HPB-specific evidence for each, and proposes a framework for matching the tool to the clinical question. A structured narrative review was performed. PubMed, Scopus, and Google Scholar were searched for studies applying PG-SGA, GLIM, or CONUT in pancreatic cancer, hepatocellular carcinoma, or biliary tract cancer. HPB-specific evidence was prioritized and the evidence supporting each tool-tumor combination was classified by directness and study design. Applied to the same populations, the tools report different prevalences and classify different patients. In the few HPB cohorts that directly compare tools, PG-SGA classified the largest proportion of patients as malnourished and is the only one of the three designed to record nutrition-impact symptoms and to guide intervention, but it is effort-dependent and may underdetect occult sarcopenia in cirrhosis. GLIM yields a criteria-based diagnosis with severity grading whose prevalence and prognostic value depend on how the muscle mass criterion is operationalized, for example from staging computed tomography. CONUT, computed from three routine laboratory values, is the least resource-intensive and is associated with survival across HPB tumor types in predominantly retrospective cohorts, but its components are confounded by hepatic dysfunction, cholestasis, and inflammation. PG-SGA, GLIM, and CONUT are complementary rather than interchangeable. Because direct comparative evidence in HPB cancer is limited, we propose a framework for matching each tool to the clinical question, tumor subtype, treatment phase and available resources, which requires prospective validation.

title: Pretreatment Serum GDF-15 and Features of Clinical Vulnerability in Advanced Pancreatic Ductal Adenocarcinoma.
abstract: Background: This study aimed to define the clinical significance of pretreatment serum growth differentiation factor-15 (GDF-15), including its associations with clinical vulnerability, survival, and chemotherapy outcomes in advanced pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC). Methods: Pretreatment serum samples were prospectively collected from 80 patients with locally advanced or metastatic PDAC. GDF-15 was measured using an enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay and analyzed continuously and according to the cohort median. Associations with clinicopathological characteristics and overall survival (OS) were evaluated in the overall cohort. Treatment effectiveness, delivery, and safety were additionally assessed among 68 patients who received systemic chemotherapy. Results: The median GDF-15 concentration was 362.6 pg/mL. Higher GDF-15 was associated with poor performance status, involvement of multiple metastatic organ sites, an elevated neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio, and hypoalbuminemia. Eleven of the 12 patients unable to receive chemotherapy because of clinical deterioration had high GDF-15. The high GDF-15 group had shorter OS than the low GDF-15 group in the overall cohort (median, 6.1 vs. 13.9 months; hazard ratio [HR] = 1.96; 95% CI, 1.23-3.13; p = 0.002). The association between continuous GDF-15 and OS was attenuated and no longer statistically significant after multivariable adjustment (HR per doubling = 1.22; 95% CI, 0.97-1.52; p = 0.085). Among treated patients, progression-free survival and objective response did not differ significantly between groups, whereas high GDF-15 was associated with shorter OS (median, 8.7 vs. 14.2 months; HR = 1.72; 95% CI, 1.02-2.90; p = 0.025) and treatment duration (median, 3.2 vs. 6.3 months; p = 0.007). Relative dose intensity and subsequent treatment rates were similar. Febrile neutropenia occurred exclusively in the high GDF-15 group, which also accounted for four of five treatment-related deaths. Conclusions: Elevated pretreatment GDF-15 was associated with limited treatment fitness and inferior survival in patients with advanced PDAC, without clear evidence of intrinsic chemotherapy resistance. GDF-15 may represent a potential marker of systemic vulnerability in advanced PDAC, although its clinical utility requires external validation.

title: Gut Microbiome Compositional and Functional Signatures Associated with Chemotherapy Response in Pancreatic Ductal Adenocarcinoma: An Exploratory Cohort Study.
abstract: Background/Objectives: The gut microbiome modulates chemotherapy efficacy in pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC), yet its relationship with the clinically relevant endpoint of post-chemotherapy surgical eligibility remains poorly characterised. We explored whether baseline gut microbiome composition and metagenomically predicted metabolic function differ between chemotherapy responders and non-responders in PDAC. Methods: In this prospective single-centre exploratory cohort study, faecal samples were collected from 15 patients with non-immediately resectable PDAC at diagnosis, before chemotherapy. Whole-genome shotgun metagenomics was performed, and microbial functional capacity was inferred through an assembly-based pipeline. Patients were classified as responders (achieved surgical eligibility, n = 6) or non-responders (n = 9). Results: At baseline, responders showed enrichment of Collinsella aerofaciens (p = 0.026) and Butyrivibrio fibrisolvens (p = 0.012), while non-responders were enriched in oral-origin bacteria (Streptococcus gordonii, Actinomyces spp., Rothia dentocariosa). Predicted butyrate showed the largest effect size difference between groups but did not reach significance (p = 0.179); responders also had broadly elevated predicted SCFAs and bile acids. However, chemotherapy regimen (mFOLFIRINOX in 5/6 responders vs. 2/9 non-responders; Fisher p = 0.041) and disease stage were unevenly distributed between groups. Conclusions: This exploratory study identifies the compositional and functional microbiome features distinguishing PDAC chemotherapy responders from non-responders. These associations are confounded by disease stage and regimen and require validation in larger, regimen-stratified cohorts before predictive or mechanistic claims can be made.

title: Prognostic and Spatial Organization of Tertiary Lymphoid Structures in Pancreatic Ductal Adenocarcinoma.
abstract: Background: Tertiary lymphoid structures (TLSs) may identify immunologically active pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC), but clinical definitions and spatial analyses have been inconsistent. Methods: We integrated a systematic review of 21 studies (22 reports) with patient-aware secondary analyses of seven public molecular datasets. Results: Pathology-defined TLS presence was associated with longer overall survival in five cohorts (1019 patients; random-effects hazard ratio 0.544, 95% confidence interval 0.398-0.743). In pathology-annotated spatial data, a mature-TLS program was enriched in TLS-positive regions at the patient level. B-cell and Tfh/CXCL13 programs showed reproducible positive associations with continuous TLS burden, whereas other program associations were less directionally consistent. An independent spatial cohort supported an rCAF-over-myCAF association with lymphoid probability. Chemokine-axis co-enrichment was observed but did not establish direct signaling. Conclusions: TLSs mark a favorable, spatially organized immune state in PDAC. The evidence supports biomarker and biological hypotheses while retaining boundaries on causality, treatment induction, and clinical prediction.

title: Current Evidence on Gene-Based and Epigenetic Therapeutic, Diagnostic, and Prognostic Strategies in Epithelial-Derived Carcinomas: A Scoping Review.
abstract: Background: Epithelial-derived carcinomas exhibit genomic instability due to genetic mutation and epigenetic dysregulation. Mechanisms such as DNA methylation, histone modifications, and noncoding RNA regulation may lead to tumor progression, immune evasion, and treatment resistance. Presently, gene-based and epigenetic therapies, including CRISPR systems, RNA interference, and chromatin-modifying agents, are reported to be effective in targeted cancer treatment. Objectives: This scoping review aims to map the evidence on gene-based technologies in epithelial-derived carcinomas, including therapeutic, diagnostic, prognostic, screening, and disease-modeling applications, and to identify molecular targets, translational outcomes, and gaps in the current evidence base. The review will characterize the molecular targets, gene-based approaches, cancer types, translational applications, and reported outcomes to identify evidence gaps, translational challenges, and priorities for future research. Methods: The scoping review was conducted as per PRISMA-ScR by conducting a literature search in databases such as PubMed, Embase, and Google Scholar, covering studies published between 2016 and 2026. In the inclusion criteria, all studies and reviews related to investigating gene-based, RNA-mediated, and epigenetic therapies in epithelial cancers were included. Thirty-six studies met the eligibility criteria. Results: Amongst the studies reviewed, the most common epithelial cancers reported were hepatocellular carcinoma, ovarian carcinoma, lung carcinoma, and pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma. Among the epithelial-derived carcinomas identified in this review, HCC was the most frequently represented cancer; epigenetic alterations and therapies used were RNA-based therapies, CRISPR diagnostics, and epigenetic drugs. Ovarian and breast cancers targeting BRCA pathways and chromatin remodeling produced clinical translation outcomes. Lung and colorectal cancers showed moderate epigenetic involvement, often managed through combined therapeutic strategies. Pancreatic cancer therapies were limited by challenges in drug delivery despite identifiable molecular targets. Gene therapies such as CRISPR-based gene editing, RNAi/siRNA therapies, miRNA/lncRNA targeting, and HDAC inhibition were commonly reported. Conclusions: The present study indicates that the majority of epithelial-derived carcinomas can benefit from gene-based and epigenetic therapies. Though the majority of carcinomas, such as hepatocellular, have good clinical outcomes, pancreatic cancer has limited clinical translation.

title: Serum Cytokine Profiling in Pancreatic Ductal Adenocarcinoma: A Pilot Study of Candidate Discriminators, Sex Differences and Altered Co-Regulation.
abstract: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) is rarely detected before the disease is advanced, and existing serum markers are insufficient for early detection. Its systemic immune alterations are incompletely characterized and rarely examined by sex. We measured 19 serum cytokines by bead-based multiplex assay in 22 patients with PDAC and 16 controls, comparing groups overall and separately in women and men, and examined co-regulation among them. In the full cohort, interleukin-7 (IL-7) was the only cytokine to discriminate patients from controls after correction for multiple testing. Adjustment for age strengthened this association, and IL-7 matched the discrimination of carbohydrate antigen 19-9 (CA19-9). After stratification by sex, IL-7 remained the only cytokine higher in women, though it did not survive correction within that subgroup, whereas in men, eight innate, T-helper 17 (Th17) and type I interferon cytokines (IL-1α, IL-1RA, IL-31, IFN-α, IL-17A, IL-17F, TNF-α, and TNF-β) separated patients from controls, although the male control group was small. The correlation network present in controls was largely absent in patients, which instead showed few associations centered on IL-2, IL-5 and IL-6. These findings identify IL-7 as a candidate discriminator of PDAC and show that the cytokines separating patients from controls differed by sex, warranting validation in a larger, sex-balanced cohort that also measures sex hormones.

title: Longitudinal Circulating Nerve Growth Factor in Pancreatic Ductal Adenocarcinoma: An Exploratory Study of Postoperative Recurrence and First-Line Disease Control.
abstract: Nerve growth factor (NGF) signaling is involved in pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) neurotropism, perineural invasion, pain, and tumor-stromal crosstalk, but its value as a circulating biomarker remains poorly defined. We retrospectively analyzed 51 patients with PDAC who underwent serial liquid-biopsy assessment across perioperative and advanced-disease timepoints. Circulating β-NGF was assessed in plasma, and samples without measurable NGF were classified as non-detectable. NGF was analyzed as both a zero-inflated continuous variable and a binary detectable/non-detectable biomarker. Phase-aligned associations with recurrence, disease-free survival, first-line progression-free survival, CA19-9, CEA, TGFβ, PD-L1, pain, and pathological perineural invasion were evaluated using non-parametric and permutation-based methods with false-discovery-rate adjustment. NGF availability was highest at first-line treatment initiation, where 9 of 40 patients had detectable NGF (22.5%). The clearest signal emerged postoperatively: patients who subsequently recurred had higher NGF values than those who did not (median 25.5 pg/mL vs. non-detectable; nominal p = 0.038). Detectable postoperative NGF was directionally associated with recurrence, while detectable NGF at first-line treatment initiation was associated with numerically shorter progression-free survival. Pooled active-disease measurements did not show a clear NGF increase versus postoperative samples, arguing against a generic disease-burden signal. No association remained significant after false-discovery-rate correction; therefore, all observed signals should be interpreted as exploratory and hypothesis-generating. These findings support prospective validation of circulating NGF within multimarker liquid-biopsy strategies focused on postoperative recurrence, perineural invasion-related biology, and treatment resistance in PDAC.

title: Diabetes and Cancer-Pathophysiology and Clinical Implications: A Systematic Review.
abstract: Diabetes Mellitus and cancer are major global health problems with rising incidence worldwide. This systematic review was conducted following PRISMA 2020 guidelines by searching PubMed, Scopus, ScienceDirect, SpringerLink, and Google Scholar for studies published between 2015 and 2026. Studies investigating the association between diabetes mellitus and cancer were selected based on predefined criteria, and data were synthesized using a narrative approach. The findings indicate a strong and mechanistically complex association between diabetes mellitus and multiple cancers, particularly pancreatic, breast, colorectal, and prostate cancers. Hyperglycemia, insulin resistance, and chronic inflammation are consistently implicated in tumor initiation and progression through key signaling pathways, including Wnt/β-catenin, PI3K/AKT/mTOR, and AMPK. A bidirectional relationship is most evident in pancreatic cancer, highlighting its unique metabolic and oncogenic interplay. Shared molecular mediators such as cytokines, microRNAs, and metabolic regulators further support a common pathogenic link. Metformin, an antidiabetic drug, demonstrated potential anticancer effects via modulation of these interconnected pathways. Overall, this review underscores a biologically intertwined relationship between diabetes mellitus and cancer, supporting the development of integrated therapeutic strategies targeting shared metabolic and signaling mechanisms.

title: A Water-Soluble Pro-Drug of Acetaminophen Has Increased Intracellular Delivery of Active Drug and Anti-Cancer Activity in Triple-Negative Breast Cancer and Pancreatic Ductal Adenocarcinoma.
abstract: Background/Objectives. Triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC) and pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) are two of the deadliest adult cancers. High-dose acetaminophen (AAP) has anti-cancer activity when given in conjunction with CYP2E1 inhibitors to block liver toxicity. However, the administration of high doses of AAP presents practical challenges stemming from limited water solubility, making it difficult to create a concentrated treatment solution in limited volume. Propacetamol (PROP) is a water-soluble AAP pro-drug that has been used clinically as an IV AAP formulation for analgesia. Methods. We sought to investigate the pharmacokinetics, safety and anti-cancer activity of PROP in comparison to AAP using transplantable syngeneic models of TNBC and PDAC. Results. In vivo, PROP was rapidly converted to AAP within minutes of administration. PROP demonstrated enhanced effectiveness in suppressing tumor growth in the TNBC and PDAC syngeneic murine tumor models compared to AAP. The enhanced efficacy of PROP appears to stem from increased cellular uptake, leading to intracellular AAP concentrations that are 2.7-fold higher within 5 min compared to cells treated with unmodified AAP. PROP demonstrated enhanced modulation of intracellular JAK/STAT signaling, a key mediator of AAP anti-cancer activity, using both murine and humanized models. STAT3 and STAT6 inhibition by PROP led to modulation of macrophage polarization, likely contributing to its anti-TNBC and anti-PDAC activity. While parenteral administration is the preferred route of administration for PROP in anti-cancer indications, we also evaluated the safety and efficacy of oral PROP in comparison to AAP. High-dose PROP demonstrated improved safety following oral administration compared to AAP in the BALB/c murine model while maintaining anti-cancer activity in vivo. Conclusions. PROP, an AAP pro-drug, demonstrates enhanced intracellular delivery of AAP and in vivo anti-cancer activity compared to unmodified AAP, setting the stage for investigation as an anti-cancer drug across different indications.

title: The Evolution of Oligometastatic Pancreatic Ductal Adenocarcinoma: From Anatomic Description to Biologically Informed Patient Selection.
abstract: Metastatic pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) has historically been managed with systemic therapy, and local therapies have, in general, been avoided in the absence of symptoms directly related to a specific metastasis. Even if a specific site of disease, such as a local recurrence, had the potential to cause symptoms in the future, there was a bias against prophylactic palliation. It was well-established that most patients die of systemic progression. This approach is now under pressure from four directions. Retrospective case series have reported survival durations longer than anticipated in highly selected patients with low-volume, single-organ disease. A randomized phase II trial reported that metastasis-directed therapy prolonged progression-free survival. Biologic data indicate that the site of metastatic relapse is encoded in gene expression profiles already present in the primary tumor. Second-line systemic therapy has become substantially more effective, which lengthens the interval over which control of an untreated metastasis may become clinically important. We trace the oligometastatic concept from the 1995 Hellman and Weichselbaum hypothesis to the 2026 OligoPanc consensus definition of up to three lesions confined to a single organ, examine the criteria proposed for patient selection, summarize the surgical and ablative radiotherapy literature, and consider the trials that will determine whether this is a treatable disease state or a favorable prognostic phenotype. We conclude that induction systemic therapy, followed by response assessment that weighs the absence of disease progression, Carbohydrate Antigen 19-9 (CA19-9) kinetics, and performance status, is a defensible route to local therapy directed at the metastases and the primary tumor, and warrants prospective study.

title: Sex Hormone Estrone Sulfate Serendipitously Downregulates Intercellular Tunneling Nanotube Conduits, EMT, and Migration in Breast and Pancreatic Cancer Cells.
abstract: Aim: Estrone (E1) is of particular interest as most breast cancers are diagnosed after menopause, the period in which E1 becomes the dominant estrogen. Triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC) is a highly invasive cancer that lacks hormone receptors for estrogen (ER), progesterone (PR), and HER2 (human epidermal growth factor receptor-2). TNBC management remains clinically challenging despite recent advances in targeted and immunotherapeutic approaches. This study investigated the effects of the estrogen hormone estrone sulfate (E1S) on cancer cells. Here, E1S engages in non-classical biased G protein-coupled estrogen receptor (GPER) signaling in TNBC MDA-MB-231 cells, estrogen receptor-positive MCF-7 breast cancer cells, and pancreatic PANC-1 cancer cells, which express estrogen, progesterone, and androgen receptors. Methods: We performed sialidase and colocalization assays in breast MDA-MB-231 and MCF-7 cells and pancreatic PANC-1 cancer cells. An epithelial-to-mesenchymal (EMT) transition, a tunneling nanotube assay, and a scratch wound assay were conducted to elucidate the cellular behaviors of E1S. We used a RawBlue reporter macrophage cell line to measure NFκB activity using the secreted embryonic alkaline phosphatase (SEAP) assay, and we measured cellular viability and metabolic activity using the AlamarBlue assay. Results: E1S induced NMBR/MMP9/Neu1 signaling in MDA-MB-231, MCF-7, PANC-1 and RawBlue cells. E1S increased E-cadherin expression, reduced N-cadherin and vimentin expression, decreased tunneling nanotube density, and reduced scratch wound migration. E1S increased SEAP activity, suggestive of increased nuclear factor-κB (NF-κB) and activator protein-1 (AP-1)-mediated transcription. E1S treatment did not affect cell viability and metabolic activity in triple-negative MDA-MB-231 breast cells using the AlamarBlue assay in a dose-dependent manner. Conclusions: E1S binding to GPER potentiates a biased heterodimerization with the GPCR neuromedin B receptor (NMBR) to activate matrix metalloproteinase 9 (MMP9) and neuraminidase 1 (Neu1), a signaling paradigm with previously established receptor tyrosine kinase (RTK) and Toll-like (TLR) receptors. Biased, temporal GPER signaling has significant implications for breast and pancreatic cancer cellular behavior, which may be leveraged to inform therapeutic strategies for aggressive forms of breast and pancreatic cancers. This research study is mechanistic in nature and may have potential translational implications.

title: Early Local Tumour Control and Feasibility of Intratumoral P-32 Microparticle Implantation in Patients with Locally Advanced Pancreatic Cancer: A Prospective Single-Center Observational Cohort Study.
abstract: Background: Evidence regarding EUS-guided intratumoral phosphorus-32 (P-32) microparticle implantation for locally advanced pancreatic cancer (LAPC) remains limited. This prospective pilot study evaluated its technical feasibility, preliminary safety, and early disease-control outcomes when administered in combination with gemcitabine plus nab-paclitaxel. Methods: Seventeen patients with unresectable LAPC underwent EUS-guided intratumoral P-32 microparticle implantation through a 22-gauge fine-needle aspiration needle during the fourth week of systemic chemotherapy. Intratumoral distribution was assessed using Bremsstrahlung SPECT/CT. Tumour response was evaluated according to RECIST version 1.1, and treatment-emergent adverse events were graded according to CTCAE version 4.0. The main secondary endpoint was local disease control rate at approximately 16 weeks (LDCR16w). All analyses were descriptive. Results: Implantation was technically successful in all 17 patients (100.0%; exact 95% CI, 80.5-100.0%), and SPECT/CT confirmed intratumoral distribution in every case. No implantation-related procedural complications were recorded (0/17; exact 95% CI, 0.0-19.5%). At approximately 16 weeks, CT assessment was available for 16 patients: seven had a partial response and nine had stable disease. The LDCR16w was 16/16 among evaluable patients (100.0%; exact 95% CI, 79.4-100.0%) and 16/17 in the all-treated analysis (94.1%; exact 95% CI, 71.3-99.9%). A reduction in CA19-9 of at least 50% was observed in 13/16 evaluable patients. Four patients underwent subsequent R0 resection (4/17, 23.5%; exact 95% CI, 6.8-49.9%). Adverse events were predominantly grade 1-2; one grade 3 abdominal pain event and no grade 4-5 events were recorded. Only three deaths occurred during a median OS follow-up of 15.6 months, making survival estimates exploratory and statistically immature. Conclusions: In this small, single-center pilot cohort of highly selected patients, EUS-guided intratumoral P-32 microparticle implantation combined with gemcitabine plus nab-paclitaxel was technically feasible and provided preliminary safety information. Because of the absence of a chemotherapy-only comparator, the small sample size, and the limited follow-up, the radiographic, biomarker, resection, and survival outcomes cannot be attributed specifically to P-32 implantation and should be considered descriptive and hypothesis-generating. Larger controlled studies with longer follow-up are required to determine clinical efficacy.

title: Urinary Biomarkers in Cancer: A Scoping Review.
abstract: Cancer remains a major global health challenge and a leading cause of mortality worldwide. As incidence continues to rise, early detection remains one of the most effective strategies for improving survival and reducing disease burden. Urine is an attractive source of biomarkers due to its non-invasive collection, ease of repeated sampling, and rich molecular composition. This scoping review evaluates the current landscape of urinary biomarkers for the early detection of cancer and their potential for clinical translation. A detailed literature search was conducted using PubMed, Embase, and Web of Science to identify studies investigating urinary biomarkers for cancer detection. Biomarkers were categorised by analyte class, and diagnostic performance, validation status, and clinical applicability were assessed. Urinary biomarkers demonstrated diagnostic potential across multiple malignancies, including lung, breast, pancreatic, hepatobiliary, colorectal, renal and ovarian cancers, while several urinary assays are already clinically available for bladder and prostate cancers. Promising diagnostic accuracy was reported for multiple biomarker classes, particularly multimarker panels integrating metabolites, proteins, nucleic acids, and epigenetic signatures. However, most studies were exploratory, involving small cohorts, methodological heterogeneity, and limited independent validation. Urinary biomarkers represent a promising and rapidly evolving approach to non-invasive cancer detection. Despite encouraging diagnostic performance, few candidates have progressed to clinical implementation. Large prospective multicentre studies, rigorous validation, and assay standardisation are essential to establish urinary biomarkers as reliable tools for cancer screening, early diagnosis, and risk stratification.

title: Incremental Prognostic Information Beyond Nodal Positivity: The AJCC 8th Edition N1/N2 Subdivision and the Lymph Node Ratio in Resected Periampullary Adenocarcinoma.
abstract: Background/Objectives: The American Joint Committee on Cancer (AJCC) 8th edition subdivides node-positive periampullary adenocarcinoma into N1 and N2 by the number of positive nodes. We quantified how much this subdivision and the lymph node ratio (LNR) each add to nodal positivity, and how the nodal yield affects the comparison. Methods: This retrospective cohort comprised 147 consecutive pancreatoduodenectomies for pancreatic head (n = 49), distal bile duct (n = 63), ampullary (n = 31) or duodenal (n = 4) adenocarcinoma. In covariate-adjusted Cox models stratified by origin, the N1/N2 subdivision and the LNR were tested over nodal positivity and over each other with nested likelihood-ratio tests, overall, with the examined-node count in the model and by the period of resection. Results: The median nodal yield was 17 (10 in 2013-2016, 19 in 2017-2024). Beyond nodal positivity, the N1/N2 subdivision added χ2 0.25 (p = 0.61; adjusted N2-versus-N1 hazard ratio 1.21, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.59-2.45) and the LNR added χ2 9.60 (p = 0.002; hazard ratio 1.41 per 0.1, 95% CI 1.22-1.62). The LNR added to the N category (p = 0.002; optimism-corrected C-index gain 0.020, 95% CI 0.002-0.041), whereas the N category did not add detectably to the LNR (p = 0.54). With the examined-node count in the model, the LNR increment was attenuated (p = 0.045) and the subdivision's increment rose (χ2 3.65, p = 0.056). From 2017 onward (n = 113), the LNR and the positive-node count were nearly collinear among the node-positive patients (ρ 0.90 versus -0.02 before 2017), and neither the subdivision (p = 0.49) nor the LNR (p = 0.17) added significantly to positivity. Conclusions: The N1/N2 subdivision added little beyond nodal positivity, although imprecisely estimated, and its increment rose when the examined-node count was in the model. The LNR added prognostic information mainly when the yield was low or variable; where the yield was higher and more uniform, the ratio and the count-based category conveyed nearly the same information, and no additional value of the ratio was demonstrated.

title: Plasma Protein Corona Fingerprinting Across Intraductal Papillary Mucinous Neoplasms and Pancreatic Ductal Adenocarcinoma: A Comparative Proof-of-Concept Study.
abstract: Background/Objectives: Surveillance of intraductal papillary mucinous neoplasms (IPMNs) provides a clinically relevant window in which biological changes associated with pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) development may potentially be investigated before advanced disease occurs. Nanoparticle-enabled protein corona (PC) fingerprinting has shown analytical potential in PDAC, but the extent to which different nanoplatforms recover distinct information across the biologically proximate IPMN-PDAC spectrum remains unclear. This exploratory study compared three nanoplatform configurations to identify a candidate workflow for subsequent validation. Methods: Plasma from 22 patients with de novo PDAC (n = 11), IPMN (n = 6), or IPMN-derived PDAC (n = 5) was incubated with graphene oxide (GO) nanosheets, gold nanoparticles (AuNPs), or cationic DOTAP-DOPE liposomes. Wash-resistant PCs were analyzed by SDS-PAGE, quantified across predefined molecular weight (MW) regions, and evaluated using exploratory linear discriminant analysis with repeated stratified cross-validation. Results: The three nanoplatforms generated non-equivalent electrophoretic PC architectures. In this small exploratory cohort, GO showed the broadest pattern of nominal clinical-group-associated variation in relative MW-region contributions and yielded internal cross-validation AUC estimates of 0.955 for IPMN versus de novo PDAC, 0.767 for IPMN versus IPMN-derived PDAC, and 0.927 for IPMN-derived versus de novo PDAC. Corresponding AUCs were 0.606-0.700 for AuNPs and 0.621-0.691 for liposomes. Conclusions: GO provided the broadest group-associated variation and numerically highest internal discrimination estimates, supporting its prioritization for independent validation and prospective longitudinal evaluation in IPMN surveillance.

title: Management Strategies for Cutaneous Adverse Events Caused by Kinase Inhibitors in Oncology: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.
abstract: The use of targeted therapies in oncology has increased significantly, but associated cutaneous adverse events often impair quality of life and adherence. Despite numerous available interventions, there is no unified protocol, and many patients discontinue therapy due to adverse events. This systematic review and meta-analysis aimed to evaluate preventive and reactive interventions for cutaneous adverse events in adult cancer patients receiving kinase inhibitors. A search was performed in MEDLINE (via PubMed), EMBASE, and CENTRAL (The Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials), using predefined search terms. Outcomes were incidence, severity of cutaneous adverse events (grades 1-4 and 3-4), quality of life and adherence to oncologic therapy. After screening 35,072 records, 9 studies (1853 patients, per protocol) met the inclusion criteria for the meta-analysis, while 52 were included in the systematic review. Preventive topical agents significantly reduced the incidence of grade 1-4 cutaneous adverse events (OR, 0.55; 95% CI, 0.38-0.80; p = 0.012; I2 = 16%), whereas systemic interventions showed no significant benefit in this category. Conversely, for grade 3-4 events, systemic interventions were associated with a significantly reduced incidence (OR, 0.24; 95% CI, 0.14-0.41; p = 0.002, I2 = 0%), while topical agents had no significant effect. For reactive interventions, no consistent evidence of effectiveness was found, with high heterogeneity and a limited number of studies. In patients receiving kinase inhibitors, systemic antibiotics were associated with a reduction in grade 3-4 cutaneous adverse events, while pooled topical interventions significantly reduced grade 1-4 events. However, the effectiveness of individual topical agents, including urea, remains uncertain.

title: Artificial Intelligence in Pancreatic Cancer: From Predictive Performance to Clinical Translation.
abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is now applied across the pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) pathway, yet the literature has grown faster than the evidence needed to act on it. The question is not whether an algorithm can predict an endpoint, but whether it yields information reliable, generalizable, and actionable enough to change a clinically meaningful decision. In this narrative, in a non-systematic review of PDAC-specific literature, we grade applications on an author-defined evidence-readiness framework (development, internal, external, prospective validation, clinical impact, and implementation) and on four dimensions-validation, comparator, actionability, and impact. Contemporary meta-analyses show high pooled accuracy for AI-based early detection and for distinguishing PDAC from mass-forming pancreatitis (sensitivity ~0.88-0.92, specificity ~0.90-0.93), but with extreme heterogeneity, low radiomics quality, scarce external validation, and-for electronic health-record risk models-positive predictive values often below 1% at population prevalence. Computed tomography (CT)-based detection and risk enrichment are among the more mature applications identified, yet none has been shown to improve stage distribution, resection rate, or survival. Treatment prediction is held to a strict standard, distinguishing prognostic association from a validated treatment-by-biomarker interaction. The rate-limiting steps are no longer algorithmic but translational-external and prospective validation, calibration, appropriate comparators, and workflow integration.

title: Bile Cell-Free DNA as a Liquid Biopsy for Biliary Tract Malignancies: A Scoping Review.
abstract: Background: Biliary tract cancers (BTCs) carry a poor prognosis driven by frequent diagnosis at advanced or metastatic stages. Inadequate tissue sampling impedes biomarker-directed selection of therapy that could potentially improve outcomes over limited chemotherapeutic options. Plasma cell-free DNA (cfDNA) yields limited sensitivity. However, given its direct contact with the tumor, bile holds promise as a locally enriched source of tumor-derived cfDNA for evaluation. Methods: Following the PRISMA-ScR guidelines, we searched PubMed/MEDLINE and EMBASE without date restrictions. Seventeen primary studies of bile cfDNA in cholangiocarcinoma (CCA), gallbladder carcinoma (GBC), pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC), and primary sclerosing cholangitis (PSC) were synthesized narratively. Results: Compared to plasma cfDNA, Bile cfDNA was isolated at higher concentrations and in longer fragments than plasma cfDNA; bile cfDNA demonstrated higher concordance with matched tumor tissue, capturing more actionable alterations. Pairing it with serum CA19-9 or newer bile-derived markers improved performance. Emerging data suggest a role in early detection of CCA during PSC surveillance. Conclusions: Bile cfDNA as a liquid biopsy medium offers analytic advantages over plasma for detecting and profiling biliary malignancy. Standardized collection, extraction, and reporting protocols and prospective multicenter validation are needed before routine use.

title: When Genomic Scars Outlive Genomic Vulnerability: Dynamic DNA Damage Repair in Cancer Evolution and Therapeutic Resistance.
abstract: Genomic biomarkers are increasingly used to identify therapeutically exploitable defects in DNA damage repair (DDR). However, genomic alterations and mutational scars largely represent the evolutionary history of a tumor, whereas therapeutic sensitivity depends on its current functional state. This distinction becomes particularly relevant during cancer progression and treatment, when selective pressure may reshape DNA repair capacity without erasing the genomic footprints generated by previous repair deficiency. Here, we examine the emerging concept of genomic scar-functional state discordance, whereby persistent genomic evidence of defective DNA repair may coexist with partial or complete restoration of repair competence. Multiple mechanisms may contribute to this transition, including secondary or reversion mutations, restoration of homologous recombination, replication fork stabilization, compensatory pathway activation, clonal selection, and epigenetic reprogramming. Conversely, initially repair-proficient tumors may acquire new DDR vulnerabilities during evolution, emphasizing the bidirectional and dynamic nature of genome maintenance. These processes challenge the assumption that a single genomic assessment can reliably define a stable therapeutic vulnerability throughout the disease course. We discuss how longitudinal approaches integrating tumor genomics, circulating tumor DNA, mutational signatures, epigenomic information, and functional measures of DNA repair could distinguish historical genomic damage from active biological dependency. Particular attention is given to gastrointestinal malignancies, including pancreatic, colorectal, gastric, and biliary tract cancers, in which DDR alterations are increasingly investigated but their predictive interpretation remains heterogeneous. We propose that precision oncology should progressively move from the concept of a static genomic biomarker toward that of a dynamic genomic state, in which therapeutic vulnerabilities are periodically reassessed as tumors evolve under treatment pressure.

title: Familial Pancreatic Cancer Associated with a Shared BRIP1 Variant: Implications for Homologous Recombination Deficiency and Targeted Therapy.
abstract: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) remains one of the most lethal malignancies, with a subset occurring in the context of hereditary cancer predisposition. BRIP1 is involved in homologous recombination repair, and pathogenic germline variants are established risk factors for ovarian cancer. However, its role in pancreatic cancer susceptibility and treatment response remains poorly defined. We report PDAC in a father and son whose tumors independently harbored the same BRIP1 p.K159E variant of uncertain significance (VUS), with clinical features suggestive of potential homologous recombination deficiency (HRD). A father and son developed PDAC at 70 and 39 years, respectively. Tumor profiling identified the same BRIP1 p.K159E VUS in both, alongside canonical PDAC-associated alterations. Germline testing was not performed. Both patients showed clinically meaningful sensitivity to platinum-based chemotherapy. The father achieved a partial response to FOLFIRINOX for early metastatic recurrence but subsequently deteriorated and died within one year of diagnosis. The son achieved prolonged disease control with platinum-based chemotherapy and multimodal treatment, including surgery and local therapies for oligoprogression, surviving approximately five years. Maintenance olaparib was briefly administered but discontinued because of hematological toxicity and subsequent disease progression. The occurrence of PDAC in two first-degree relatives, including early-onset disease in the son, together with the same BRIP1 p.K159E VUS in both tumors, represents an unusual familial and molecular observation. Although germline status and pathogenicity cannot be established, the shared alteration and platinum sensitivity raise the hypothesis that this BRIP1 variant may warrant further investigation in the context of homologous recombination repair. However, platinum sensitivity alone cannot be considered evidence of homologous recombination deficiency. The uncertain benefit from PARP inhibition further highlights the limitations of inferring therapeutic actionability from an individual HRR gene VUS. Further germline and functional investigation of BRIP1 alterations in PDAC is warranted.

title: Immunohistochemical Expression of M30, BCL-2, BAX, and Ki-67 in Pancreatic Ductal Adenocarcinoma: Association with Clinicopathological Features.
abstract: Background: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) is an aggressive malignancy with limited survival despite advances in diagnosis and treatment. Dysregulation of apoptosis and tumor cell proliferation is a fundamental feature of cancer biology. M30, BCL-2, and BAX reflect different aspects of apoptotic activity and regulation, whereas Ki-67 is a widely used marker of cellular proliferation. However, the clinicopathological significance of these markers in PDAC remains incompletely characterized. This study aimed to evaluate the immunohistochemical expression of M30, BCL-2, BAX, and Ki-67 in PDAC and to investigate their associations with established clinicopathological features. Methods: This retrospective study included 50 patients with surgically resected PDAC treated at Afyon Kocatepe University Medical Faculty Hospital between January 2003 and May 2015. Archived tumor specimens were evaluated by immunohistochemistry for M30, BCL-2, BAX, and Ki-67. M30 and Ki-67 expression were quantified according to the percentage of positive tumor cells, while BCL-2 and BAX expression were assessed using semiquantitative staining scores based on staining intensity and the proportion of positive tumor cells. Immunohistochemical findings were compared with sex, tumor differentiation, tumor size, lymphovascular invasion, perineural invasion, surgical margin status, tumor stage, lymph node metastasis, and clinical stage. Results: The study cohort comprised 30 male and 20 female patients, with a mean age of 62.12 ± 10.93 years. M30 expression was detected in 39 (78%) cases, whereas Ki-67 expression ranged from 10% to 85% of tumor cells. BCL-2 and BAX expression showed variable staining patterns. None of the four markers demonstrated a statistically significant association with tumor differentiation, tumor size, lymphovascular invasion, perineural invasion, surgical margin status, tumor stage, lymph node metastasis, or clinical stage. Conclusions: In this cohort of surgically resected PDAC, immunohistochemical expression of M30, BCL-2, BAX, and Ki-67 was not significantly associated with conventional clinicopathological indicators of tumor aggressiveness. These findings indicate that immunohistochemical assessment of individual apoptosis- and proliferation-related markers may not adequately reflect tumor aggressiveness or clinicopathological heterogeneity in PDAC. Further studies incorporating larger cohorts, standardized immunohistochemical assessment, and clinical outcome data are warranted to clarify their potential biological and prognostic significance.

title: Histopathological Spectrum and Yield of Advanced Neoplasia in Opportunistic Colonoscopy Without Organised Screening: A Single-Centre Cross-Sectional Study from Western Romania.
abstract: Background/Objectives: Organised colorectal cancer screening is still being introduced in Romania, and the yield of opportunistic colonoscopy outside it is poorly documented. Our primary aim was to describe the histopathological spectrum and the yield of advanced neoplasia in an opportunistic colonoscopy service; a secondary, exploratory aim was to describe self-reported lifestyle items in a questionnaire subgroup. Methods: This study represents a retrospective cross-sectional analysis of consecutive colonoscopies (June 2023-June 2024) at a county hospital outside organised screening, restricted to patients from whom material reached histopathology; the comparison group therefore comprises patients whose sampled lesions were benign, not patients without neoplasia. Advanced neoplasia was defined histologically as adenocarcinoma or adenoma with high-grade dysplasia, without the 10 mm size criterion. A convenience subgroup self-completed a locally developed, unvalidated questionnaire before the procedure; its items were tested against advanced neoplasia and adenocarcinoma with false discovery rate correction. Results: Among 274 patients, 45 (16.4%) had adenocarcinoma, 139 (50.7%) adenoma and 72 (26.3%) advanced neoplasia; per examination (n = 978), detection was 4.6% for adenocarcinoma and 7.4% for advanced neoplasia.
