Forty-four of 45 carcinomas were graded as moderately differentiated, and no serrated lesion was separately reported. Age was associated with advanced neoplasia (OR 1.34 per decade, 95% CI 1.01-1.79). Questionnaire data were available for only 79 patients (28.8%), among whom adenocarcinoma was more frequent than among non-respondents (26.6% vs. 12.3%). In this subgroup, obesity was inversely (OR 0.07, 95% CI 0.02-0.28) and reported weight loss positively (OR 6.77, 2.26-20.30) associated with advanced neoplasia, and two coffee items were inversely associated; processed meat, dairy, aspirin and supplement use were not associated after correction. Conclusions: Opportunistic colonoscopy at this centre recovered a high proportion of carcinoma, consistent with symptom-driven presentation, and the reporting of serrated lesions and tumour grade requires standardisation. The questionnaire findings rest on a small, selected subgroup and are hypothesis-generating only. The inverse obesity association is most plausibly explained by selection of the comparison group and of respondents, and none of the associations identifies a risk factor.

title: Graph Neural Network Modelling of Pre-Diagnostic Serum Proteomics for Pancreatic Cancer Detection.
abstract: Background/Objectives: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) has exceptionally high mortality, largely because of late diagnosis, while established blood biomarkers such as CA19-9 have limited sensitivity for early detection. We evaluated whether modelling serum proteomic measurements as supervised pairwise statistical graphs using synolitic graph neural networks (SGNNs) could provide a useful framework for pre-diagnostic PDAC classification. Methods: We analysed 217 pre-diagnostic serum samples from UKCTOCS, comprising 100 PDAC samples from 75 women and 117 control samples, profiled for 97 proteins. Samples were divided into a development set collected 0-1 year before diagnosis (n = 110) and a temporal holdout set collected 1-2 years before diagnosis (n = 107); 25 PDAC participants contributed samples to both windows. The final SGNN used fold-internal mutual-information selection of 30 proteins, pairwise RBF-SVM-derived edge information, minimum-connected sparsification, and a 10-member GATv2 ensemble per cross-validation fold. Conventional machine-learning comparators were tuned using development data only. Results: The SGNN achieved a mean 5-fold development ROC-AUC of 75.33 ± 10.43%, lower than the tuned Random Forest (81.67%); the other tuned comparators achieved 77.67% (XGBoost), 77.17% (logistic regression), and 73.17% (SVM). Averaging predictions across the five-fold-specific SGNN ensembles yielded a temporal-holdout ROC-AUC of 64.35% (95% CI 52.6-74.6%). In the participant-independent subset of 25 PDAC cases not represented in development and 57 controls, ROC-AUC was 66.04% (95% CI 52.56-78.88%). Conclusions: SGNNs provide a feasible graph-based representation of pre-diagnostic proteomic data but did not outperform optimised conventional machine-learning methods within development cross-validation. The temporal and participant-independent performance estimates warrant further investigation in larger fully independent cohorts. A graph-specific predictive advantage was not directly tested-no such advantage was demonstrated in this dataset-and the clinical utility has not been established.

title: Genomic Differences Between Corticotroph and Ectopic ACTH-Producing NETs.
abstract: We aimed to identify and compare key molecular alterations underlying adrenocorticotropin (ACTH)-producing neuroendocrine tumors (NETs) in Cushing's disease and ectopic ACTH syndrome. Whole-exome sequencing was performed on 34 pituitary ACTH-secreting NETs (corticotroph tumors: 30 microadenomas and 4 macroadenomas) and 8 ectopic ACTH-producing NETs of lung, pancreatic, and renal origin. Somatic point mutations, copy-number alterations, and loss of heterozygosity (LOH) were compared between corticotroph and ectopic ACTH-producing NETs. Corticotroph tumors demonstrated significantly more gene deletions and LOH events compared with ectopic ACTH-producing NETs (median 1687 and 2573.5 affected genes in corticotroph tumors, respectively). In corticotroph tumors recurrent subtelomeric deletions and LOH on chromosome 19 affecting FAM98C, RASGRP4, RYR1, MAP4K1, and EIF3K were observed. Notably, TERT deletion was detected in 94% of corticotroph tumors versus only 12.5% ectopic ACTH-producing NETs. In contrast, ectopic ACTH-producing NETs frequently exhibited chromosomal duplications on chromosomes 17 and 21, enriched for keratin-associated protein gene clusters. Recurrent somatic point mutations were identified in BRAF, CACNA1I, KLHL20, MCCC2, LRP1, TCP11X2, USP8, and USP48 genes, explaining the molecular basis of disease in 20 of 34 corticotroph tumors and 2 of 6 lung ACTH-producing NETs (LRP1 R1497Q and CACNA1I S639T). These findings indicate that corticotroph tumors predominantly demonstrated deletions and LOH involving subtelomeric genes, whereas ectopic ACTH-producing tumors more commonly exhibited chromosomal duplications. Potentially relevant somatic mutations were detected in 59% of corticotroph tumors and in 33% of lung ACTH-producing NETs. In conclusion, ACTH-producing NETs of pituitary versus other localizations demonstrate significantly different genetic alterations despite similar clinical and secretory phenotypes.

title: Recent advances in scaffold-based KRAS<sup>G12C</sup> inhibitors: SAR and biological evaluation insights.
abstract: Over the past decade, targeting Kirsten rat sarcoma viral oncogene homolog (KRAS) mutations has shifted from being considered an undruggable target to becoming a realistic therapeutic strategy with the development of KRASG12C inhibitors. This mutation replaces glycine with cysteine at codon 12, thereby reducing the GTPase activity by keeping the protein in its active GTP-bound state. This process activates downstream RAF-MEK-ERK and PI3K-AKT signalling pathways and plays a crucial role in driving various cellular processes such as uncontrolled cell proliferation and survival in cancers, including non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC), colorectal cancer, and pancreatic cancer. In the present review, various KRASG12C inhibitors reported in the last five years are compiled according to their structural class, including quinazolines, pyrimidines, pyrido-pyrimidinones, and pyrrole-pyrimidines, along with PROTAC-based degraders. Among these, compound 12 exhibited strong antiproliferative activity against the KRASG12C-mutant H358 cell line with an IC50 value of 7.6 nM. The presence of a 2-fluorophenyl moiety made compound 12 the most active compound. Compound 18 was also identified as a highly effective PROTAC degrader with IC50 = 0.045 μM (45 nM) in MIA PaCa-2 cells. Structure-activity relationship (SAR) analysis demonstrated that electrophilic warheads (acrylamide moieties) together with rigid heterocyclic scaffolds play a key role in enhancing potency and selectivity. Additionally, docking studies, biological evaluations, and in vivo findings are discussed to provide a clearer picture of the therapeutic potential of various KRASG12C inhibitors. Overall, the present review highlights the recent progress in the development of KRASG12C inhibitors for the treatment of cancer.

title: From macrofungal polysaccharides to precision microbial immunotherapy: reprogramming the tumor microenvironment through immunometabolic and gene-regulatory pathways.
abstract: Engineered microbial immunotherapies can localize immune-modulating signals within solid tumors, where hypoxia, suppressive myeloid cells, deficient antigen presentation, and dysfunctional T-cell trafficking often limit immunotherapy. Macrofungal polysaccharides, especially structurally defined β-glucans, offer mechanistic templates rather than interchangeable drug substances for source-specific, structure-controlled immune engineering programs. Their activity depends on linkage, branching, molecular mass, conformation, solubility, aggregation, and physical presentation. Critically, the strongest Dectin-1 and trained-immunity evidence discussed here uses particulate β-glucans from Saccharomyces cerevisiae; those findings cannot be assigned directly to macrofungal β-glucans without material-specific comparison. We therefore distinguish four engineering architectures: de novo microbial biosynthesis of a defined β-glucan, microbial surface display, delivery of a pre-characterized β-glucan cargo, and delivery of non-glycan payloads that mimic the desired downstream immune program. Because therapeutic bacteria have not yet been shown to reproduce a macrofungal β-glucan with controlled linkage, branching, conformation, and presentation, near-term development should prioritize standardized cargo delivery or pathway mimicry. In pancreatic and colorectal cancer models, yeast whole-glucan particles have altered myeloid trafficking or generated epigenetically and metabolically trained macrophages linked to CXCL9/CXCL10 production, natural killer-cell recruitment, conventional type 1 dendritic-cell accumulation, and stronger CD8 T-cell responses. Human evidence remains preliminary and cannot establish β-glucan-specific efficacy in uncontrolled combination studies. This Perspective proposes source-resolved material characterization, receptor and cell-state testing, multidimensional pharmacodynamic biomarkers, and microbial safety controls as prerequisites for translating fungal-inspired immune programs into precision cancer therapeutics.

title: Tumor-educated macrophages promote ferroptosis inhibition in pancreatic cancer via activating the p62-KEAP1-NRF2 pathway.
abstract: Pancreatic cancer is one of the most aggressive and lethal gastrointestinal malignancies, and ferroptosis resistance contributes to chemoresistance. Tumor-educated macrophages(TAMs) are key components of the tumor microenvironment, but whether and how they regulate ferroptosis in pancreatic cancer cells remains largely unknown. This study aimed to investigate the regulatory role of tumor-educated macrophages (TEMs) in pancreatic cancer cell ferroptosis and the underlying molecular mechanism. TEMs were generated by coculturing THP-1 cells with the pancreatic cancer cell lines PANC1 and CFPAC, and TEM-conditioned medium (TEM-CM) was collected to treat pancreatic cancer cells. Ferroptosis was induced by erastin, and ferroptotic events were assessed by lipid ROS, MDA, iron accumulation, GSH levels, and transmission electron microscopy. RNA sequencing was performed to identify differentially expressed genes. The expression and activity of VEGFR2, C-Raf, ERK1/2, mTOR, LC3, p62, KEAP1, and NRF2 were investigated by treating cells with pharmacological inhibitors (Ki8751, LY3009120, chloroquine, and ferrostatin-1), performing gene knockdown and overexpression, and conducting Western blot co-immunoprecipitation, ubiquitination, and cycloheximide chase assays. In vivo experiments were conducted using an orthotopic mouse model of pancreatic cancer (n = 5 per group). TEM-CM reduced the sensitivity of PANC1 and CFPAC cells to erastin-induced ferroptosis, as evidenced by decreased lipid ROS, MDA, and iron accumulation and increased GSH levels. Neutralization of VEGF, but not IL-10 or TGFβ, significantly reversed the ferroptosis-inhibiting effect of TEM-CM. RNA sequencing identified TM7SF2 as a key mediator. TEM-CM upregulated TM7SF2 mRNA and protein levels, activated mTOR, and suppressed autophagy, leading to p62 accumulation. Accumulated p62 competitively bound KEAP1, disrupted the KEAP1-NRF2 interaction, inhibited NRF2 ubiquitination and degradation, and promoted NRF2 nuclear translocation, thereby upregulating GPX4, HMOX1, and GCLM. Mechanistically, TEM-derived VEGF bound VEGFR2 and activated the C-Raf/ERK1/2 pathway by upregulating TM7SF2, which in turn promoted mTOR phosphorylation. These effects were reversed by TM7SF2 knockdown, VEGF neutralization, VEGFR2 inhibition, or C-Raf inhibition. These findings suggest that TEM-derived VEGF promotes ferroptosis resistance in pancreatic cancer cells through the VEGFR2-TM7SF2-C-Raf/ERK1/2-mTOR-autophagy-p62-NRF2 axis. This axis may represent a potential therapeutic target for overcoming ferroptosis resistance in pancreatic cancer. However, our conclusions are mainly based on in vitro cell models, and further validation in additional cell lines, patient-derived organoids, and in vivo models is warranted.

title: Microbial-derived metabolites in cancer: evidence boundaries, immune mechanisms and translational pathways.
abstract: Microbial metabolites can suppress or promote tumor development and modify treatment response, but the direction of an effect depends on its chemical identity, anatomical source, concentration and host target. This narrative review critically examines short-chain fatty acids, tryptophan derivatives, secondary bile acids, colibactin, cyclic dinucleotides and microbial activities that alter anticancer drugs. We distinguish individual metabolites from postbiotic preparations, microbial components and enzymes, and separate microbial production from host-microbial co-metabolism. Mechanistic examples include butyrate-dependent chromatin regulation, macrophage aryl hydrocarbon receptor signaling, microbial agonists of STING, colibactin-induced DNA cross-links and bacterial conversion of gemcitabine or irinotecan metabolites. For each, we consider the experimental model, evidence for causality, physiological exposure and limits of human translation. Particular attention is given to apparently conflicting short-chain-fatty-acid findings across checkpoint inhibitors, the conditional effects of dietary fiber, and discordance between experimental drug inactivation and human pancreatic tumor profiling. Human studies support selected biomarker associations and early intervention feasibility, including fecal microbiota transplantation and engineered bacterial delivery, but do not establish a general metabolite-based treatment strategy. We therefore propose a seven-step research framework linking patient sampling, direct quantification and source attribution, causal and functional testing, external biomarker validation, intervention selection, pharmacodynamic monitoring and prospectively defined clinical endpoints. Its contribution is to make the evidence required for each translational decision explicit while distinguishing clinically useful prediction from a causally justified intervention.

title: Treating a systemic disease as a local one: failure points of current pancreatic cancer management and a multimodal, biology-guided framework for redesign.
abstract: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma remains among the most lethal solid tumors, with 5-year survival near 13% despite decades of incremental change, and current management continues to be organized around anatomic resectability and a chemotherapy backbone applied largely without regard to tumor biology. This article advances the thesis that the dominant paradigm underperforms because it treats a systemic, molecularly convergent, multi-compartment disease as though it were a local one. We first summarize the real advances of the past decade-in surgery, systemic therapy, molecular profiling, and immunotherapy-and then identify five interlocking failure points that persist despite them: (i) selection by vessel anatomy, judged on imaging criteria that are read inconsistently and that classify inaccurately even where read consistently, and applied to splanchnic veins without accounting for their baseline variability and tumor-associated thrombosis; (ii) occult metastasis and the resulting limits of local cure for the systemic majority, evidenced by the gap between complete resection and durable survival and by early distant recurrence; (iii) the addition of radiotherapy, which improves local control without extending survival; (iv) chemotherapy chosen without reference to a validated prognostic classical/basal-like distinction, although prospective subtype-directed regimen selection has not yet improved outcomes in randomized testing; and (v) a sequential, non-integrated structure in which systemic and immune therapy are deferred and no definitive path exists for the roughly 80% who are not surgical candidates. We then propose a multimodal, biology-guided framework that answers each failure point, with every component graded on an explicit evidence scale: corrected tumor-suppressor gene therapy matched to lesion type, a systemic backbone combining renin-angiotensin system-pathway inhibition with immunogenically sequenced chemotherapy and personalized neoantigen vaccination, in-situ immune conversion of an accessible tumor by cryoablation with local priming and natural killer (NK) cell delivery, and front-end biological patient selection. The framework is conceptual rather than product-specific; we specify its rationale, its integration in time, a staged first-in-human development program, and the studies required to test it. The objective is to convert local disease into systemic benefit-a step the current paradigm is not designed to take.

title: Histotripsy in tumor therapy: advances in non-thermal mechanical ablation, immune modulation, and clinical translation.
abstract: Histotripsy is an emerging non-invasive focused-ultrasound technology that mechanically disrupts tissue through controlled bubble activity rather than sustained thermal coagulation. This review distinguishes shock-scattering cavitational histotripsy, intrinsic threshold histotripsy, and boiling histotripsy and relates their pulse regimes, bubble dynamics, tissue effects, monitoring strategies, and evidence maturity. Mechanical fractionation can expose tumor antigens and damage-associated molecular patterns, but immune outcomes vary by submodality, dose, tumor model, treated fraction, and sampling time; no standardized head-to-head evidence establishes a superior immunological approach. Early prospective liver studies demonstrate high technical feasibility and encouraging local control, whereas post-market cohorts also reveal targeting limitations and uncommon but clinically important vascular, thrombotic, and renal complications. Pancreatic investigation remains ongoing, while the renal CAIN study is completed with registry results and a peer-reviewed first-patient report. A clinically useful dosimetry framework should connect delivered acoustic parameters with in situ cavitation, tissue disruption, imaging or acoustic surrogates, and delayed oncologic and immune endpoints. Histotripsy should currently be viewed as a complementary local therapy with a distinctive mechanical mechanism rather than as a proven replacement for established ablation. Standardized reporting, independently adjudicated safety data, and prospective comparative trials are needed to define its durable oncologic and immunological value.

title: Metabolic sensing in 3D models of pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma: probing pH, oxygen, and lactate dynamics to decode chemoresistance.
abstract: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) is one of the deadliest malignancies due to its late diagnosis, extensive desmoplasia, and strong chemoresistance. Recent advances in three-dimensional (3D) in vitro modelling have provided new insights into tumor-stroma interactions and metabolic adaptations that drive disease progression. This review summarizes the pathogenesis and tumor microenvironment (TME) hallmarks of PDAC, emphasizing the metabolic heterogeneity characterized by altered pH, oxygen, and lactate gradients. It discusses conventional and emerging therapeutic strategies, the molecular basis of drug resistance, and the role of the TME in treatment failure. Furthermore, it highlights the evolution of 3D experimental models as physiologically relevant tools to study PDAC biology and evaluate drug efficacy. Special attention is given to the integration of optical biosensors for non-invasive spatio-temporal monitoring of pH and metabolic fluctuations. These sensing technologies, coupled with advanced bioengineered models, are paving the way for precision oncology and patient-tailored strategies in pancreatic cancer.

title: Case Report: Isolated leptomeningeal relapse after systemic control in PALB2-altered pancreatic cancer.
abstract: Leptomeningeal metastasis (LM) is an uncommon manifestation of pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) and has a median survival of only 1-2 months after diagnosis. Isolated LM after prolonged extracranial disease control is particularly rare and may be overlooked when systemic imaging results look stable. We describe a 51-year-old man with metastatic PDAC who initially received a treatment regimen comprising KN046 and gemcitabine and nab-paclitaxel, followed by a prolonged course of folinic acid, fluorouracil, irinotecan, and oxaliplatin (FOLFIRINOX), and subsequently underwent conversion surgery with a pathological complete response (ypT0N0, R0). Several months after completing adjuvant FOLFIRINOX, the patient developed a new right lower limb weakness. Brain MRI and cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) cytology results confirmed the presence of isolated LM, but there was no evidence of active extracranial disease. CSF sequencing identified Kirsten rat sarcoma viral oncogene homolog G12D, an AT-rich interaction domain 1A frameshift alteration, and a truncating partner and localizer of BRCA2 p.L920* alteration involving the homologous recombination repair (HRR) pathway. Then, the patient underwent ventriculoperitoneal shunt and Ommaya reservoir placement, followed by treatment with serial intrathecal methotrexate plus dexamethasone and systemic toripalimab with bevacizumab. This multimodal approach was followed by temporary neurological stabilization, but the disease eventually progressed. He survived approximately 30 months since the initial PDAC diagnosis and 3.5 months after LM diagnosis. Together with our review of 29 published PDAC-LM cases, this report suggests two recurring clinical patterns: fulminant presentation at/or near initial diagnosis and delayed central nervous system (CNS) relapse after prolonged systemic disease control. The repeated detection of Fanconi anemia/homologous recombination repair pathway alterations in several genomically characterized cases gives rise to the possibility that treatment-responsive, HRR pathway-altered PDAC may survive long enough for CNS sanctuary relapse to become clinically apparent. CSF genomic profiling may help characterize rare CNS relapse in molecularly defined PDAC, and new neurological symptoms in long-surviving patients warrant prompt evaluation even when extracranial disease appears controlled.

title: Global and registry-based patterns of pancreatic cancer: GLOBOCAN 2020, CI5plus trends (2000-2017), and demographic projections to 2040.
abstract: Pancreatic cancer is a highly lethal malignancy for which mortality remains close to incidence. We combined complementary global estimates and longitudinal cancer-registry data to characterize its current burden, recent incidence trends, and demographic implications to 2040. GLOBOCAN 2020 was used for cross-sectional estimates of pancreatic cancer incidence and mortality in 185 countries and territories. Continuous annual incidence trends from 2000 to 2017 were estimated from selected non-overlapping CI5plus registry populations with complete coverage over the study period. Age-standardized rates were calculated using the Segi-Doll world standard population. Log-linear models and continuous segmented regression selected by the Bayesian information criterion were used to estimate annual percentage changes (APCs). IARC Cancer Tomorrow fixed-risk demographic projections were used to estimate incident cases through 2040; annual risk-change scenarios of -0.5% and +0.5% were examined as sensitivity analyses. In 2020, an estimated 495,773 pancreatic cancer cases and 466,003 deaths occurred worldwide; the ASIR and ASMR were 4.86 and 4.53 per 100,000, respectively, and the mortality-to-incidence ratio was 0.94. Northern America and Europe had the highest regional ASIRs (8.04 and 7.77), whereas Asia contributed the largest number of cases (233,701). In pooled selected CI5plus populations, incidence increased during 2000-2006 (APC 1.43%, 95% CI 1.27-1.59) and 2006-2017 (APC 1.02%, 95% CI 0.94-1.10). The relative increase was greatest among adults younger than 50 years (APC 1.61%, 95% CI 1.37-1.85), although their absolute rate remained low. Under the fixed-risk demographic scenario, global incident cases were projected to reach 843,772 in 2040, a 70.2% increase from 2020. Pancreatic cancer imposes a substantial and geographically unequal burden, with mortality remaining close to incidence. Combining GLOBOCAN with CI5plus distinguishes contemporary global burden from observed registry-based trends and supports risk-based surveillance, registry strengthening, and health-system capacity planning.

title: Type 1 and 2 subclassification may be a promising approach to evaluate intraductal papillary neoplasm and intraductal oncocytic neoplasm of the bile duct.
abstract: In the pancreatobiliary system, precursor lesions are traditionally classified as low-grade dysplasia (LGD) or high-grade dysplasia (HGD), a scheme widely applied to pancreatic precursors. However, applying this system to biliary precursors, including intraductal papillary neoplasm of the bile duct (IPNB) and intraductal oncocytic papillary neoplasm of the bile duct (bIOPN), presents several challenges: (i) virtually all IPNBs and bIOPNs contain variable foci of HGD; (ii) lesions composed entirely of LGD and associated with a favorable clinical course may not exist; and (iii) virtually all IPNBs and bIOPNs are managed clinically as malignant tumors at diagnosis. Accordingly, a type 1/2 subclassification was proposed on the basis that HGD can be divided into traditional HGD and HGD with irregular and complicated lesions (ICLs), irrespective of LGD. Type 2 IPNB/bIOPN exhibits traditional HGD with ICLs, whereas type 1 exhibits traditional HGD without ICLs. Type 1 IPNB/bIOPN shares many features with prototypic pancreatic and ampullary intraductal tumoral precursors, whereas type 2 differs to varying degrees from these prototypes. Subsequent studies have demonstrated the superiority of this subclassification over traditional two-tiered grading, with moderate interobserver agreement, and have identified additional clinicopathological features of IPNB/bIOPN. Importantly, type 2 is associated with less favorable postoperative overall survival than type 1. The type 1/2 subclassification may therefore provide a useful framework for clarifying the clinicopathological and molecular/genetic features of IPNB/bIOPN.

title: USP22-mediated phagocytic evasion promotes immune escape in TP53-inactivated hepatocellular carcinoma.
abstract: Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) is characterized by an immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment. Here, we aimed to elucidate the tumor cell-intrinsic functions of ubiquitin-specific protease 22 (USP22) in the immune escape of HCC cells. Autochthonous mouse models of HCC with either genetic Usp22 loss or Trp53 knockdown were used. In vitro and in vivo phagocytosis assays were performed to evaluate the interactions between HCC cells and macrophages. Multicolor fluorescence, spatial transcriptomics, immunoprecipitation and ubiquitination assays were used to explore the potential underlying mechanisms. We observed that tumor cell-intrinsic USP22 inhibits the infiltration and anticancer function of tumoricidal macrophages in HCC. USP22 expression in HCC cells blocks their direct phagocytosis by tumoricidal macrophages. Mechanistically, CD24 (a known phagocytosis checkpoint) mediates USP22-induced suppression of phagocytosis. USP22 promotes the transcriptional expression of CD24 by deubiquitinating and stabilizing the transcription factor E2F7. Furthermore, wild-type p53 downregulates USP22 protein expression, whereas TP53 inactivation markedly upregulates USP22 protein expression. The USP22-E2F7-CD24 axis is responsible for mediating TP53-inactivation-induced phagocytic evasion and hepatocarcinogenesis. Mechanistically, USP22 proteins bind to one another and suppress ubiquitination at the K442 residue. The wild-type p53 protein disrupts this mutual deubiquitination, thereby facilitating USP22 degradation. Moreover, TNF secreted by tumoricidal macrophages promotes USP22 degradation by disrupting its self-stabilizing mechanism in a wild-type p53-dependent manner. Our findings indicate that USP22-E2F7-CD24 axis-mediated phagocytic evasion promotes immune escape in TP53-inactivated HCC.

title: Impact of ERCP on pancreatitis frequency in pediatric acute recurrent or chronic pancreatitis: An INSPPIRE-2 study.
abstract: Treatment options for pediatric acute recurrent pancreatitis (ARP) and chronic pancreatitis (CP) are limited. We aim to quantify the response rate to endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography (ERCP) and identify predictive factors that determine response in children with ARP or CP. Data was obtained from the INternational  Study Group of  Pediatric  Pancreatitis:  In search for a cu RE-2 cohort who underwent ERCP. ERCP response was defined as a decrease in acute pancreatitis (AP) attacks by 50% in the year after first ERCP, compared to the year before this ERCP. Fisher's exact test was used to assess associations between categorical variables and Wilcoxon rank-sum test or two-sample t-test for continuous variables. There were 436 children who underwent a total of 1504 ERCPs in our cohort. Eighty-five patients (19.5%) had ARP; 351 (80.5%) had CP. Significant differences were noted between those who had ERCP and those who did not based on sex, BMI percentile and diagnosis. ERCP response rate was 70.0% (n = 206). Patients with pancreatic duct calculi/obstruction were more likely to be ERCP responders (p < 0.04). ERCP was used commonly in the treatment of ARP/CP for children with any pancreatic duct abnormality. Two-thirds of children responded well to endoscopic therapy with at least 50% decrease in AP attacks the year post-initial ERCP; ductal calculi/obstruction were associated with higher rate of response. These results support that therapeutic ERCP is safe and may provide short to medium-term therapeutic benefit in children with ARP or CP especially with ductal factors seen on pre-intervention imaging.
journal: Journal of pediatric gastroenterology and nutrition

title: Exosome-Inspired Proteolipid Nanoparticles Enable Safe, Extrahepatic RNAi-Chemo Therapy Through Cholesterol-Free, Tumor-Preferential Delivery.
abstract: Lipid nanoparticle (LNP)-enabled genetic medicines are reshaping cancer therapy yet remain constrained by liver-biased tropism, dose-limiting toxicities, and limited efficacy in refractory solid tumors such as pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC). Here, exosome-inspired proteolipid nanoparticles (Em-pLNPs) are developed to embed three exosomal membrane proteins within an ionizable lipid matrix to support safe, extrahepatic delivery of combinatorial gene-chemo payloads. Em-pLNPs are generated by one-step microfluidic mixing to incorporate the tetraspanins CD63 and CD81 and the "don't-eat-me" marker CD47 into the lipid shell, co-encapsulate diverse nucleic acid and small-molecule cargos, and enable modular CD44-targeted surface functionalization. Following systemic administration in orthotopic PDAC models, Em-pLNPs exhibit prolonged circulation, preferential extrahepatic tumor accumulation, deep penetration of desmoplastic stroma, and efficient cytosolic delivery, while markedly improving tissue tolerability relative to ligand-decorated clinical LNP benchmarks. Formulated with an RNAi-chemo cocktail (siKRAS, siIL-6, and gemcitabine), Em-pLNPs permit repeated intravenous dosing that drives robust, synergistic tumor regression and mitigates chemoresistance. By coupling exosome-like immune evasion and tissue tropism with the manufacturability and high gene-loading capacity of LNPs, Em-pLNPs define a translational proteolipid platform for safe extrahepatic gene therapy against refractory solid tumors.

title: Second Primary Malignancies After Appendiceal Neuroendocrine Tumors: A Contemporary SEER-Based Standardized Incidence Ratio Analysis (2015-2023).
abstract: Whether contemporary appendiceal neuroendocrine tumor (NET) survivors have an increased risk of second primary malignancies (SPMs) remains uncertain. We assessed relative incidence and the effect of excluding early post-diagnosis events. We identified adults aged ≥20 years with malignant appendiceal NETs diagnosed between 2015 and 2023 in Surveillance, Epidemiology, and End Results (SEER) data from 17 registries. Observed and expected SPMs were compared using standardized incidence ratios (SIRs). The primary analysis excluded events occurring within the first two months, with sensitivity analyses using ≥6- and ≥12-month exclusion periods. The baseline cohort included 4,854 patients. At ≥2 months, 4,522 patients contributed 18,273.65 person-years, with 119 observed SPMs compared with 103.03 expected SPMs (SIR, 1.15; 95% CI, 0.96-1.38). Elevated estimates were observed for malignancies of the digestive system (SIR, 1.56; 95% CI, 1.03-2.27), pancreas (2.51; 1.01-5.17), kidney and renal pelvis (2.36; 1.08-4.49), and thyroid (2.73; 1.36-4.89). Overall SIRs were 1.15, 1.10, and 1.03 across the three exclusion thresholds. Several site-specific estimates decreased, but pancreatic SIRs remained similar (2.51, 2.70, and 2.58). No site-specific confidence interval excluded unity at ≥12 months. Overall SPM incidence was not significantly elevated. Early site-specific findings warrant caution because of small event counts, multiple comparisons, and possible detection effects that SEER cannot directly measure. Loss of statistical significance with longer exclusion periods does not exclude persistent site-specific excess incidence. These results do not support additional routine organ-directed screening solely based on appendiceal NET history.
journal: Asian Pacific journal of cancer prevention : APJCP

title: Time to Treatment Initiation and Risk of Metastatic Progression in Pancreatic Ductal Adenocarcinoma.
abstract: The association between time to treatment initiation (TTI) and metastatic progression in pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) remains poorly characterized. We evaluated the association between TTI and subsequent metastasis among patients undergoing curative-intent resection for PDAC. Medicare Fee-for-Service beneficiaries aged ≥ 66 years with nonmetastatic PDAC who underwent curative-intent resection from 2017 to 2021 were identified. TTI was defined as the interval from diagnosis to first cancer-directed treatment and modeled continuously per 30-day increase. Three-year metastatic progression was evaluated using Fine-Gray competing-risks regression, with death before metastasis as a competing event. Each 30-day increase in TTI was independently associated with a 14.2% higher subhazard of metastasis (subdistribution hazard ratio [sHR], 1.142; 95% CI, 1.119-1.166; p < 0.001). The association persisted across surgery alone (sHR, 1.130), neoadjuvant therapy followed by surgery (sHR, 1.187), surgery followed by adjuvant therapy (sHR, 1.144), and trimodality therapy (sHR, 1.125) (all p < 0.001). In sensitivity analysis restricted to TTI ≤ 90 days, the association was attenuated and not statistically significant (sHR, 1.064; 95% CI, 0.964-1.174; p = 0.22). Longer TTI was associated with increased metastatic progression across treatment pathways, although this association was attenuated among patients with TTI ≤ 90 days. Further studies are needed to determine whether treatment timing independently influences metastatic progression.

title: A Case With Longitudinal Changes in Apolipoprotein A2 Isoform Indices Associated With CA19-9 and MRI Findings Until Pancreatic Cancer Development.
abstract: An 80-year-old female was referred to our hospital 6 years earlier with an abnormal plasma apolipoprotein A2 isoform (ApoA2-i) index, which is a promising biomarker for pancreatic cancer. Endoscopic ultrasonography (EUS) revealed a single small cystic lesion in the pancreatic head. Subsequently, the patient was followed up regularly. Two years after the initial visit, her ApoA2-i index was 50.2 μg/mL, and her plasma CA19-9 level was 42.5 U/mL. Magnetic resonance cholangiopancreatography (MRCP) performed 3 years after the initial visit also demonstrated small cystic lesions in the pancreatic head, consistent with the findings of the initial EUS, and a signal defect in the main pancreatic duct (MPD) in the pancreatic body, with a normal upstream MPD diameter. Her ApoA2-i index was 52.4 μg/mL, and her plasma CA19-9 level was 42.0 U/mL. Follow-up MRCP indicated similar cystic lesions in the pancreatic head and a signal defect in the MPD in the pancreatic body, with a normal upstream MPD diameter. However, her serial ApoA2-i indices gradually decreased from 52.1 to 35.7 μg/mL, correlated with an increase in plasma CA19-9. The latest MRCP demonstrated a similar signal defect and dilatation of the upstream MPD diameter compared with the previous MPD diameters. Her ApoA2-i index slightly decreased to 35.2 μg/mL, whereas her CA19-9 level remarkably increased to 1320 U/mL. Endoscopic retrograde pancreatography with cytology demonstrated adenocarcinoma cells. In the present case, we observed longitudinal changes in ApoA2-i indices correlated with CA19-9 and MRCP findings.

title: Fibroblast-myeloid stromal crosstalk is associated with clinicopathological diversity in intraductal papillary mucinous neoplasms of the pancreas.
abstract: Intraductal papillary mucinous neoplasm (IPMN), a grossly visible precursor of pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma, is classified into gastric, intestinal, and pancreatobiliary subtypes, each associated with distinct clinicopathological features and biological aggressiveness. We hypothesised that the tumour microenvironment can explain the association between histological subtypes and clinical outcomes. We first enrolled 116 IPMN resection cases, with or without associated invasive carcinoma, and then sequenced four single-nucleus RNA-sequencing (snRNA-seq) libraries from those with distinct histological grades and subtypes. The snRNA-seq revealed that fibroblasts were the main source of cell-cell communication, whereas myeloid and mast cells were the main receivers. Therefore, we subclassified fibroblasts into inflammatory (iCAF), myofibroblast (myCAF), and reticular-like (rCAF) subpopulations, and myeloid cells into monocytes, neutrophils, macrophages, and dendritic cell subpopulations. Cell-cell interaction analysis revealed that iCAF and rCAF mainly communicated with SPP1<sup>High</sup> macrophages via the C3-integrin pathway and with neutrophils via the CXCL12-CXCR4 pathway, whereas myCAF mainly communicated with monocytes and mast cells via ECM-related pathways. Subsequently, we performed two panels of Opal multiplex immunohistochemistry and Elastic van Gieson staining to evaluate fibroblast and myeloid subpopulations and collagen, respectively, in all enrolled cases. Quantitative image analyses revealed that iCAF, neutrophils, and SPP1<sup>+</sup> macrophages were associated with higher histological grade, whereas myCAF, collagen, monocytes, and mast cells were associated with lower histological grade. No decrease in myCAF or increase in neutrophils was observed in the invasive intestinal type. Finally, we classified the cases into three groups based on the density of fibroblast and myeloid subpopulations: iCAF/SPP1<sup>+</sup> macrophage-rich (I-stroma), neutrophil-rich (N-stroma), and myCAF/mast cell-rich (M-stroma). These stromal groups were associated with distinct clinicopathological features. In conclusion, we revealed that the heterogeneous microenvironment of IPMN, associated with distinct clinicopathological features, may explain the clinical significance of histological subtypes. © 2026 The Pathological Society of Great Britain and Ireland.

title: Comparative characterization of OncoPro™ and Wnt-based media reveals distinct phenotypic and pharmacologic states in patient-derived tumor organoids.
abstract: Patient-derived tumor organoids (PDTOs) are strongly influenced by culture medium. We compared OncoPro™ (OP) Tumoroid Culture medium with conventional Wnt/R-spondin/noggin (Wnt) medium. This recently developed OP medium offers a standardized, serum-free alternative to Wnt-based formulations. We compared OP and Wnt media across 36 PDTO lines from various malignancies (colorectal, pancreatic, breast, lung, gastric, gastroesophageal junction, biliary head and neck and unknown primary), assessing establishment success. Selected PDTO models were subjected to downstream characterization, including morphological assessment and bulk transcriptomic profiling with comparison to public single-cell RNA sequencing reference datasets (n = 11), whole-exome sequencing (WES) (n = 9), and pharmacological response profiling to a 33-drug panel (n = 3). Adaptation from Wnt medium to OP succeeded in 83.3% (15/18), whereas de novo establishment favored Wnt (33.3% vs 11.1%). Key oncogenic driver alterations were retained across matched organoid cultures, supporting preservation of tumor-relevant genomic features. Transcriptomic profiling confirmed preserved tumor-identity across media, while revealing different epithelial state programs: Wnt upregulated proliferation/stemness-associated genes (e.g. LGR5) and OP enriched adhesion-associated genes and inflammatory/TGF-β programs. In scRNA databases OP signatures preferentially mapped to malignant epithelial compartments in pancreatic cancer, whereas Wnt signatures were linked to non-malignant epithelium. Similarly, in colon cancer OP signature mapped predominantly to the malignant epithelial compartments. Drug (n = 33) screening in pancreatic- and colorectal cancer PDTOs (n = 3) demonstrated consistent medium-dependent shifts: Wnt-grown PDTOs were globally more sensitive in the screened subset, particularly to MAPK-axis inhibitors and apoptosis-sensitizers, while OP-grown PDTOs exhibited relative resistance. Culture medium composition is a key determinant of PDTO phenotype, transcriptome and drug sensitivity. Wnt medium was associated with drug-sensitive states, whereas OP medium was associated with adhesion- and inflammatory-related programs, relative resistance in the screened subset of 33 drugs and closer alignment with malignant epithelial programs in the analyzed pancreatic / colorectal cancer single-cell atlases.

title: Stromal CCL2/CXCL10/SPARC axes drive pro-tumor CHI3L1 expression for microenvironmental modulation in pancreatic cancer progression and therapeutic innovation.
abstract: Chitinase-3-like-protein 1 (CHI3L1), a low-abundance protein in normal tissues, is markedly upregulated in the pancreatic tumor microenvironment (TME), where it promotes fibrosis and immune evasion. Spatial transcriptomics revealed enrichment of CHI3L1 at tumor-stroma interfaces, suggesting that cell-cell interactions regulate CHI3L1 expression. We employed 2D and 3D multicellular culture models, incorporating pancreatic cancer cells, macrophages, and pancreatic stellate cells (PSCs), to recapitulate TME-mediated CHI3L1 induction. Mechanistic insights were gained through secretome profiling, chromatin immunoprecipitation (ChIP), and methylation-specific PCR. The therapeutic potential of targeting identified axes was evaluated in an orthotopic pancreatic adenocarcinoma (PDAC) mouse model. We identified CCL2, CXCL10, and SPARC as key secreted mediators during tumor-stroma crosstalk that cooperatively induced CHI3L1 expression in cancer cells via activation of NF-κB and STAT3. Specifically, inflammatory cytokines within the TME recruited macrophages to induce CCL2, which, in concert with PSCs, enhances CXCL10 and SPARC secretion. Mechanistically, NF-κB directly bound the CHI3L1 promoter, while STAT3 reduced DNA methyltransferase 1 levels, leading to promoter hypomethylation and epigenetic activation of CHI3L1. Clinically, high CHI3L1 expression correlated with the upregulated stromal CCL2, CXCL10, and SPARC levels, and the combined four-marker signature was an independent prognostic factor for both overall and disease-free survival in multivariable analysis. In vivo, blockade of the upstream stromal pathways (CCR2/CXCR3/TGFβR1) coupled with CHI3L1 neutralization reduced tumor growth and remodeled the immunosuppressive microenvironment in immunocompetent PDAC models. Our findings uncover a cooperative multicellular signaling network that orchestrates CHI3L1 expression in cancer via transcriptional and epigenetic reprogramming. Disrupting these upstream stromal pathways concurrently with CHI3L1 neutralization was associated with reduced T-cell exhaustion, offering a promising combinatorial approach for PDAC immunotherapy.

title: Rethinking evidence generation in gastrointestinal cancer treatment research: the need for both high-quality interventional and observational evidence.
abstract: The current research ecosystem on gastrointestinal (GI) cancers-including anal, colorectal, esogastric, pancreatic, hepatocellular, and biliary tract cancers-relies heavily on randomized controlled trials (RCTs), which involve high costs and limited transportability. Fewer than 10% of therapeutic recommendations for pancreatic adenocarcinoma are based on high-level evidence, a proportion that has not improved between 2011 and 2022. Furthermore, substantial research waste undermines interventional research in GI cancer: 30-37% of completed GI cancer trials lack publicly available results, and only 59% of gastric cancer trials are published as full-text articles. Such waste in research negatively impacts evidence synthesis and guidelines recommendations. While interventional research is the only way to assess the efficacy of a new drug, observational studies and real-world evidence (RWE), using health records, cohorts, registries and/or administrative databases, may offer complementary insights, especially for research questions that cannot be studied by RCTs. In particular, RWE can evaluate treatments in elderly or comorbid patients often excluded from trials, inform decisions for rare tumors such as digestive neuroendocrine neoplasms, and evaluate real-world effectiveness of treatments such as targeted therapies or immunotherapy. While historically RWE reliability was often criticized for biases and data quality issues, methodological advances, such as target trial emulation and data standardization, have enhanced its validity, and it is now increasingly used to support regulatory decisions by agencies like the Food and Drug Administration and the European Medicines Agency. Better integration of high quality interventional and observational approaches is essential in GI cancer research. Guidance on when to use interventional versus observational studies, depending on the clinical question, may help put this integration into practice. This synergy could reduce research waste, accelerate evidence generation, and help identify more effective personalized treatments for GI cancer patients.

title: Burdens of pancreatic cancer from 1990 to 2021 and projection to 2050 in China: findings from the 2021 global burden of disease study.
abstract: Pancreatic cancer in China exhibits high incidence and mortality rates, and they have been on a continuous upward trend over time, imposing a significant disease burden. It is essential to clarify the trends in pancreatic cancer from 1990 to 2021 and predict future trends up to 2050, which can provide valuable information for planning effective management and prevention strategies. The pancreatic cancer data from 1990 to 2021 were obtained from the Global Health Data Exchange (GHDx) query tool. In this study, the incidence rate, mortality rate, disability-adjusted life years (DALYs), and related risk factor data of pancreatic cancer in China from 1990 to 2021 were extracted. The age-period-cohort (BAPC) Bayesian model was adopted to predict the age-standardized rate trend of the disease burden from 2021 to 2050, and the uncertainty of the historical estimation of GBD was incorporated into the prediction. Trend analysis uses Joinpoint regression to calculate the average annual percentage change. The model parameter Settings (such as the maximum number of connection points and prior distribution) and the standard population basis all follow the norms to ensure the comparability and repeatability of the results. In 2021, the number of incident cases, deaths, and Disability-Adjusted Life Years (DALYs) showed an increasing trend, reaching 118,665.43 cases (94,622.75-144,663.08), 119,601.86 cases (95,653.59-145,218.13), and 2,930,317.01 cases (2,301,048.70-3,575,078.95) person-years, respectively. Over the 30-year period, the Average Annual Percentage Change (AAPC) for incidence, deaths, and DALYs were 3.13% (3.08-3.18), 3.06% (2.79-3.33), and 2.53% (2.31-2.75), respectively. The Age-Standardized Incidence Rate (ASIR), Age-Standardized Death Rate (ASMR), and Age-Standardized DALY Rate were 5.64 per 100,000 (4.52-6.84), 5.72 per 100,000 (4.59-6.91), and 137.23 per 100,000 (108.15-166.74), respectively. However, from 1990 to 2021, the average age-standardized incidence, death, and DALY rates in China increased by 2.14% (1.27-3.19), 2.08% (1.22-3.10), and 1.62% (0.87-2.52), respectively. Analysis of risk factors for pancreatic cancer revealed that from 1990 to 2021, high fasting plasma glucose surpassed smoking as the leading risk factor, with high body-mass index ranking third. Gender-specific analysis showed that incidence, mortality, and DALY rates were higher in males than females. Population data projections from 2021 to 2050 indicate that the actual disease burden of pancreatic cancer in the next 30 years may be higher than the predicted value in this study. This study comprehensively compares differences in the disease burden across populations and over time, providing further evidence for the development of pancreatic cancer prevention and control policies and etiological research.

title: Proof-of-concept study toward the automated evaluation of surgical skills in laparoscopic liver resection using artificial intelligence.
abstract: Maintaining a dry surgical field is fundamental to safe laparoscopic hepatectomy (LH); however, formal certification systems rely on labor-intensive expert review of unedited surgical videos. This study evaluated the association between AI-derived blood pixel count (BPC), which quantifies redness of the hepatic transection plane, and Endoscopic Surgical Skill Qualification System (ESSQS)-based surgical proficiency, and assessed its discriminatory performance for Low-score and Failed videos. We retrospectively analyzed 146 LH videos submitted to the ESSQS of the Japan Society for Endoscopic Surgery in 2020-2021. Bleeding regions were segmented using DeepLabv3+. BPC was calculated as the total number of pixels classified as bleeding across all sampled frames. Outcomes were Pass/Fail classification using the 70-point cutoff and the Low-score group, defined as ESSQS scores ≤ mean - 1 standard deviation. ROC analysis assessed discrimination. A BPC threshold with specificity ≥90% was selected. The median BPC was 1,741,749 pixels (range, 7,944-10,507,218). BPC increased monotonically from the High-score group to the Low-score group (P < 0.001), and the Failed group had higher BPC than the Passed group (P = 0.001). The AUC of BPC was 0.708 (95% CI, 0.599-0.817) for identifying the Low-score group and 0.648 (95% CI, 0.546-0.751) for identifying the Failed group. Using a BPC threshold of 4,794,565 pixels, specificity and sensitivity for Low-score identification were 90.2 and 29.2%, respectively. In low-difficulty cases, the AUC for identifying the Low-score group was 0.784. When the same threshold was applied to Pass/Fail classification, no Passed video had a BPC at or above the threshold. AI-based BPC was associated with ESSQS-based surgical proficiency in LH. This objective, scalable, high-specificity metric may help flag procedures warranting expert review and timely feedback, particularly in low-difficulty cases. External validation and prospective implementation studies are warranted.

title: Length of stay and nhi-reimbursed expenditures after robotic-assisted surgery in taiwan: a nationwide population-based study.
abstract: Population-level evidence comparing robotic-assisted surgery (RAS) with laparoscopic surgery (LS)/video-assisted thoracoscopic surgery (VATS) and open surgery (OS) across multiple procedures from a payer perspective remains limited. This study aimed to compare postoperative length of stay (LOS) and insurer-reimbursed in-hospital expenditures among RAS, LS/VATS, and OS across representative procedures following the expansion of RAS reimbursement in Taiwan. This retrospective nationwide population-based cohort study was conducted using claims data from Taiwan's National Health Insurance Research Database. We identified adults (age ≥ 18 y) who underwent 1 of 12 representative procedures spanning thoracic, hepatobiliary-pancreatic, colorectal, urologic, and gynecologic specialties between September 1 and December 31, 2024. Surgical approaches were classified as robotic-assisted surgery (RAS), laparoscopic or video-assisted thoracoscopic surgery (LS/VATS), or open surgery (OS) using the corresponding procedure and robotic-assistance codes in the NHI claims database. The outcomes were postoperative LOS and total NHI-reimbursed in-hospital expenditures excluding special medical materials during the index hospitalization. Procedure-specific stabilized inverse probability of treatment weighting was applied to each pairwise comparison. This study included 17 549 patients. Of these patients, 2900, 9763, and 4886 underwent RAS, LS/VATS, and OS, respectively. RAS was associated with a significantly shorter postoperative LOS than LS/VATS for lung resection, colectomy, partial nephrectomy, and nephroureterectomy and with lower reimbursed expenditures for lung resection, partial pancreatectomy, nephroureterectomy, and radical prostatectomy. Compared with OS, RAS was associated with a significantly shorter postoperative LOS for selected procedures, with the largest difference noted for colectomy (8.38 vs. 14.80 d). Moreover, RAS was associated with lower reimbursed expenditures than OS for lung resection, minor hepatectomy, partial pancreatectomy, colectomy, and malignant hysterectomy. During the early period following the September 2024 expansion of NHI reimbursement for RAS in Taiwan, RAS was associated with shorter postoperative LOS for selected procedures, whereas differences in NHI-reimbursed in-hospital expenditures excluding special medical materials varied by procedure and comparator. Given the observational study design, residual confounding, and limited propensity-score overlap in several comparisons, particularly RAS versus OS, these findings should be interpreted as procedure-specific associations rather than evidence of clinical or economic superiority.

title: Body image distress in women and men with advanced pancreatic cancer approaching death - post-hoc analyses from the MISTRAL-trial.
abstract: Weight loss is common in individuals with pancreatic cancer. The aim of the present study was to address how body image distress and weight worries change over time as death approaches in patients with pancreatic cancer, and whether there are gender differences. Post-hoc analyses were performed using data from the MISTRAL-trial. Body image distress and weight worries were assessed using the European Organisation for Research and Treatment of Cancer (EORTC) QLQ-PAN-26-questionnaire as part of the original trial. Data were used to assess body image distress and weight worries at time points corresponding to 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, and 6 months prior to death. Mixed-effects linear models with random intercepts were used to examine trajectories of body image distress and weight worries in women and men. We analysed data from 125 participants, of whom 64 (51.2%) were women. Both body image distress and weight worries increased over time during the 6 months preceding death, β = 3.54, 95%CI: 1.67- 5.41; and β = 2.98, 95%CI: 0.53- 5.44, respectively. There were no statistically significant sex differences in the rate of change although women tended to report higher body image distress closer to death and men higher weight worries across all time points. Increased body image distress and weight loss concerns observed in both women and men with pancreatic cancer at the end of life highlight the importance of addressing these issues in palliative care.
journal: Supportive care in cancer : official journal of the Multinational Association of Supportive Care in Cancer

title: Mitophagy-dependent mitochondrial DNA release links ionizing radiation to immunogenic cell death in pancreatic cancer.
abstract: Ionizing radiation (IR) elicits both cytotoxic and immunomodulatory effects, yet the precise link between mitochondrial remodeling and immunogenic cell death (ICD) remains elusive. Here, we report that IR triggers robust mitophagy in pancreatic cancer cells, marked by mitochondrial damage, Parkin/BNIP3 upregulation, and increased autophagic flux. In parallel, IR induces key hallmarks of ICD, including calreticulin exposure, HMGB1 translocation, and the release of ATP and IFN-β. Notably, genetic or pharmacological inhibition of mitophagy attenuated this immunogenic profile, whereas mitophagy induction amplified it. We further demonstrate that mitophagy triggers the cytosolic release of mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) to activate immune signaling, which can be reversed by blocking mtDNA replication. In murine models, Parkin overexpression enhanced mitophagy and ICD marker expression, leading to reduced tumor burden and prolonged survival following irradiation. Collectively, our findings indicate that mtDNA leakage downstream of mitophagy links mitochondrial remodeling to radiation-induced ICD, suggesting that modulation of mitochondrial dynamics may represent a strategy to enhance both radiosensitivity and the immunogenic potential of radiotherapy in pancreatic cancer.

title: Hereditary Pancreatitis.
abstract: There are multiple genetic defects associated with hereditary pancreatitis, which have variable penetrance. Important genes include PRSS1, serine protease inhibitor Kazal type 1, and cystic fibrosis transmembrane conductance regulator. Disease pathogenesis is typically through trypsin dysregulation, intracellular stress, or altered pancreatic duct physiology. There is considerable variability in epidemiology, clinical manifestation, and prognosis between the known variants. Management should include environmental risk factor modification, monitoring for endocrine and exocrine insufficiency and malnutrition, screening for pancreatic cancer if appropriate, and a multidisciplinary approach to address long-term complications and quality of life for patients and families.

title: Hereditary Pancreatic Cancer.
abstract: Pancreatic cancer remains one of the deadliest malignancies, with most patients presenting at advanced stages and experiencing poor survival outcomes. Approximately 10% to 15% of cases are associated with inherited genetic susceptibility, highlighting the critical role of germline genetic testing and family history assessment. Multiple hereditary cancer syndromes, including those involving BRCA1, BRCA2, ATM, PALB2, CDKN2A, STK11, TP53, and select Lynch syndrome mismatch repair genes, confer increased risk of pancreatic cancer. Universal germline testing, cascade testing of at-risk relatives, and individualized risk assessment facilitate precision oncology and early detection. Screening for pancreatic cancer using select imaging modalities enables earlier-stage diagnosis and improves survival.

title: Patient-Derived Organoids from cryopreserved tissue can represent clinically relevant tools for drug testing in Biliary Cancer.
abstract: Patient-derived organoids (PDO) are three-dimensional cultures established from cancer tissues. While PDOs can replicate morphology and drug sensitivity of cancer from given patients, their clinical applicability is limited by their lack of integration in clinical trials. We aimed to define the establishment rate of PDOs from patients with cholangiocarcinoma (CCA) and establish a protocol for the generation of PDOs from cryopreserved tissue. We established a biobank of PDOs from tumour tissues (N=26). A protocol for organoid establishment from cryopreserved tissue was optimised in mice, confirmed in human PDO, and validated across institutions. While we started from a wide enrolment of different subtypes, including Pancreatic cancer (N=7), CCA (N=11), duodenal (N=2) and Ampullary Cancer (N=6), we refined the protocol towards biliary phenotype, with reduced efficiency rate in intestinal phenotype cancers. In total, 15 PDOs were established (58%); in the CCA cohort the efficiency rate of 75% (8 out of 11). Confirmation of organoid tumour origin was achieved through pathology review within a clinically-relevant time frame [median: 1.6 months (0.43-4.83 months)]. There was no numerical enrichment of successful PDO establishment for CCAs with poor prognostic factors such as perineural invasion, vascular invasion, nodal status and resection margins (p>0.05). Data from drug screening was ready within an average of 3 months from tissue collection (range:1.4-3.4 months). PDO from cryopreserved tissue was successful in 67% of cases and maintained the morphology, secretory functions, kinetic and dynamic growth patterns, transcriptomics, and drug sensitivity compared to organoids established from fresh tissues. Cryopreserved tissue can facilitate the centralisation of PDO establishment and thus, the integration of biliary PDOs in multicentric trials.

title: MUC16 drives macrophage-mediated immunosuppression in pancreatic cancer.
abstract: Mucin-16 (MUC16) is overexpressed in >60% of pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) cases and correlates with poor outcomes, yet its role in regulating tumor-immune interactions remains incompletely defined. Using KPC and KPC-MUC16 knockout (KPC-MUC16<sup>KO</sup>) genetically engineered and orthotopic mouse models, we show that loss of MUC16 markedly reduces tumor burden and reprograms the tumor microenvironment (TME) toward a less immunosuppressive state. MUC16 deficiency significantly decreased CD206<sup>+</sup> and Ym1/2<sup>+</sup> M2-like macrophages, increased the M1/M2 ratio, and improved survival. Cytokine profiling identified CCL2 and Serpin-E1 as MUC16- dependent secreted factors that promote macrophage recruitment and polarization; neutralization of these cytokines reduced macrophage migration in vitro. Bone marrow-derived macrophages (BMDM) exposed to MUC16-expressing tumor cells or conditioned media adopted a CD206<sup>+</sup>Arg1<sup>+</sup> M2-like phenotype, whereas MUC16<sup>KO</sup> tumor signals favored inflammatory CD86<sup>+</sup>iNOS<sup>+</sup> M1-like polarization. Macrophage depletion using clodronate liposomes significantly impaired tumor growth in MUC16-competent tumors but had minimal effect in KPC-MUC16<sup>KO</sup> tumors, indicating dependence on macrophage-mediated immunosuppression in the former group. Spatial transcriptomics revealed a globally distinct TME in MUC16<sup>KO</sup> tumors, including enhanced antigen-presentation programs, increased complement activation, and fibroblast states skewed toward pro-inflammatory signaling. These findings establish MUC16 as a key orchestrator of macrophage-driven immunosuppression in PDAC and support therapeutic strategies combining MUC16-targeted interventions with TME-reprogramming approaches.

title: Frailty and home time loss after surgical resection for patients with non-metastatic pancreatic cancer.
abstract: Home time, conceptualized as days alive outside of inpatient medical settings, captures dimensions of care obscured by traditional measures such as morbidity and mortality. For patients with pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC), home time loss is particularly meaningful given the poor prognosis and substantial morbidity following pancreatectomy. The relation between frailty and home time loss in this population has not been evaluated. Using SEER-Medicare data (2013-2022), we identified patients ≥66-years-old undergoing pancreatectomy for non-metastatic PDAC. We classified patients preoperatively as non-frail, pre-frail, or frail using the Claims-Based Frailty Index. We defined home time loss as cumulative days lost to hospitalization, skilled nursing facility (SNF) admission, or death in the year post-pancreatectomy. We used negative binomial regression to estimate the association between frailty and home time loss, adjusting for sociodemographic and clinical factors. Among 4553 patients (median age 74), 44.3% were non-frail, 47.9% pre-frail, and 7.8% frail. One-year mortality was 31.7% (non-frail: 26.9%; pre-frail: 33%; frail: 51.1%). Mean home time loss was 83.8 days (hospitalization: 19.0; SNF: 7.4; death: 57.5). Among days alive, the percentage spent hospitalized was 3.6% in non-frail, 4.7% in pre-frail, and 7.7% in frail patients (p < 0.001). Compared with non-frail patients, pre-frail patients lost 23% more days at home (p < 0.001) and frail patients lost 86% more days (p < 0.001); this association persisted across hospital and SNF use. Frailty is strongly associated with home time loss in the year after curative-intent pancreatectomy and warrants careful consideration during shared decision-making for patients with non-metastatic PDAC contemplating surgery.

title: Pancreatic mucinous cystic neoplasms in adults: An update on the role of CT and MRI for risk stratification.
abstract: Pancreatic mucinous cystic neoplasms (MCNs) are characterized histologically by an inner mucin-producing columnar epithelium supported by a dense ovarian-type stroma. MCNs account for approximately 10% of pancreatic cystic neoplasms. Surgical resection is the treatment of choice, as MCNs may harbor high-grade dysplasia or progress to invasive carcinoma. Establishing reliable imaging criteria for risk stratification is critical to identify patients who are candidates for surgery. Computed tomography and magnetic resonance imaging play pivotal roles in lesion characterization and assessment of features associated with high-grade dysplasia or invasive carcinoma. Current guidelines recognize several imaging features as high-risk characteristics for MCNs, including large tumor size, mural nodules, and main pancreatic duct dilatation. However, other potential predictors of malignancy remain poorly defined and are not sufficiently emphasized. The strongest MCN-specific evidence, as demonstrated in multivariable analyses, supports larger cyst size, mural nodules, main pancreatic duct dilatation, and, in selected cohorts, elevated serum cancer antigen 19-9. Male sex has also been associated with malignancy in retrospective surgical cohorts, whereas pancreatic head/neck location, calcification, wall/septal thickening, age, and signal heterogeneity on T2-weighted images remain less consistently validated. Importantly, most malignancy-prediction literature is based on resected, pathologically confirmed MCNs and is therefore vulnerable to selection and verification bias and cannot be directly extrapolated to all incidentally detected presumed MCNs. This article presents a transparent literature search methodology and an evidence-based synthesis of predictors of malignancy that clearly distinguishes MCN-specific multivariable evidence from lower-level or extrapolated data. It also provides a comparison of key guidelines. Unlike previous reviews, this article directly addresses the evidence gap between resection-based cohorts and the broader population of incidentally detected presumed MCNs. It also clarifies when imaging findings should prompt further evaluation rather than independently determine management.

title: FOLFIRINOX vs. gemcitabine/nab-paclitaxel for metastatic pancreatic cancer: A real-world study.
abstract: FOLFIRINOX and gemcitabine/nab-paclitaxel are widely used first-line regimens in metastatic pancreatic cancer (mPC); however, direct real-world comparisons and clear criteria for selecting between the two remain limited. In this retrospective cohort study, we used a multicenter real-world data registry to compare outcomes between patients with mPC treated with FOLFIRINOX and gemcitabine/nab-paclitaxel and explore associations between genomic alterations and survival outcomes. The cohort included patients with mPC treated with FOLFIRINOX (n = 272) or gemcitabine/nab-paclitaxel (n = 280) between 2010 and 2022 at tertiary referral cancer centers. The primary outcomes were overall and progression-free survival. Available next-generation sequencing results were used to explore potential prognostic biomarkers. The FOLFIRINOX group was significantly younger than the gemcitabine/nab-paclitaxel group. Before propensity score matching, the FOLFIRINOX group showed significantly longer median overall and progression-free survival. Afterward, survival outcomes no longer significantly differed. Next-generation sequencing panel data were available for 57 and 29 patients in the FOLFIRINOX and gemcitabine/nab-paclitaxel groups, respectively. In the gemcitabine/nab-paclitaxel group, ARID1A and RNF43 mutations were correlated with shorter progression-free survival. Genomic alterations in the TGF-β pathway were associated with longer overall survival with gemcitabine/nab-paclitaxel. No statistically significant differences in OS or PFS were observed between FOLFIRINOX and gemcitabine/nab-paclitaxel after propensity score matching. The exploratory genomic associations require validation in larger prospective cohorts before their potential role in treatment selection can be established. This work was supported by grants from the National Research Foundation of Korea (RS-2024-00,335,625, RS-2024-00,342,475, and NRF-2021R1A2C1008898), Korea Evaluation Institute of Industrial Technology (20,023,781), and Korea Health Technology R&D Project through the Korea Health Industry Development Institute (HI22C047400).

title: Japanese women surgeons-Past, present, and future.
abstract: Japan presents a unique cultural and medical context. While the number of male surgeons across various surgical fields declined significantly from 2014 to 2022, the number of women surgeons rose rapidly during the same period. Japanese surgeons typically face long working hours and low pay. Women surgeons also perform fewer operations, particularly high-difficulty surgeries, but handle more high-risk patients, whereas short-term outcomes show no surgeon gender differences. The 2024 work style reform for physicians capped overtime duties up to 1,860 hours per year, but the definition of "work" remains ambiguous. Generational attitudes toward domestic work are shifting; 76% of surgeons, regardless of gender, in their 20s accept sharing household chores, and more surgeons are choosing work with fewer responsibilities. The increase in women surgeons is encouraging amidst the overall decline. Work style reforms are crucial to ensure women overcome barriers like child rearing to thrive. Surgical societies are actively promoting gender equality and increasing the appointment of women to decision-making bodies. Increasing women in leadership must be fair and transparent. Indispensable leadership training for younger generations is required to effectively voice the opinions they represent.

title: TRIALSCOPE - A Framework for Clinical Trial Simulation from Real-World Data.
abstract: The rapid digitization of real-world data presents an unprecedented opportunity to optimize health care delivery and accelerate biomedical discovery. However, these data are often found in unstructured forms, such as clinical notes in electronic medical records (EMRs), and are typically plagued by confounders, making it challenging to generate robust real-world evidence (RWE). Therefore, we present TRIALSCOPE, a framework designed to distill RWE from population-level observational data at scale. TRIALSCOPE leverages biomedical language models to structure clinical text at scale, employs advanced probabilistic modeling for denoising and imputation, and incorporates state-of-the-art causal inference techniques to address common confounders in treatment effect estimation. Extensive experiments were conducted on a large-scale dataset of over 1 million cancer patients from a single large health care network in the United States. TRIALSCOPE was shown to automatically curate high-quality structured patient data, expanding the dataset and incorporating key patient attributes only available in unstructured form. The framework reduces confounding in treatment effect estimation, generating comparable results with randomized controlled lung cancer trials. In addition, we demonstrate simulations of unconducted clinical trials - including a pancreatic cancer trial with varying eligibility criteria - using a suite of validation tests to ensure robustness. Thorough ablation studies were conducted to better understand key components of TRIALSCOPE and establish best practices for RWE generation from EMRs. TRIALSCOPE was able to extract cancer treatment data from EMRs, overcoming limitations of manual curation. We were also able to show that TRIALSCOPE could reproduce the results of lung and pancreatic cancer clinical trials from the extracted real-world data.

title: Probing Spatiotemporal pHi and pHe Dynamics in Tumor Spheroids during Growth and Alkaline Therapy via Surface-Enhanced Raman Spectroscopy.
abstract: The acidic microenvironment in solid tumors is not merely a metabolic byproduct of the Warburg effect but actively promotes disease aggressiveness and treatment failure. Tumor alkalization therapy, which aims to neutralize or alkalinize the TME, has therefore emerged as a promising adjunct to conventional cancer treatments. In this study, we fabricated both SERS nanosensors and microsensors for parallel spatiotemporal monitoring of intracellular pH (pHi) and extracellular pH (pHe) within tumor spheroids derived from three human cancer cell lines: lung adenocarcinoma (H1975), pancreatic cancer (SW1990), and colorectal cancer (SW480). Over a 7-day culture period, distinct pHi and pHe profiles were observed among the different cell types. We then examined the pH modulation elicited by administration of sodium bicarbonate (NaHCO3), a clinically employed alkaline agent. Exposure to 75 mM NaHCO3 for 24 h induced a marked elevation of pHe (∼0.78 units) and a modest increment in pHi (∼0.37 units). This integrated nanosensor-microsensor system, which leverages the size effect for precise spatial localization, offers a versatile approach for elucidating the complex interactions within the tumor microenvironment and helps optimize pH-modulating cancer therapies.

title: SLC25A39: A key regulator of mitochondrial metabolism and a promising therapeutic target in cancer.
abstract: The mitochondrial solute carrier (SLC25) family regulates solute transport across the mitochondrial inner membrane. Among them, SLC25A39 has emerged as a critical player in tumor biology, primarily through its dual role in mediating mitochondrial glutathione (mGSH) transport and maintaining iron-sulfur cluster homeostasis. Recent evidence implies that SLC25A39 dysfunction disrupts mGSH metabolism, thereby influencing iron-sulfur cluster synthesis and driving metabolic reprogramming in tumors. Notably, SLC25A39 is governed by a GSH-Fe-S-AFG3L2 feedback circuit, a feature not shared by its closest homolog SLC25A40. Additionally, upregulation of SLC25A39 is frequently observed in multiple malignancies, including colorectal, pancreatic, and liver cancers, where it correlates with enhanced proliferation, metastasis, and poor prognosis. Furthermore, SLC25A39 expression is intricately associated with remodeling of the tumor immune microenvironment and the development of therapeutic resistance, although these associations are primarily based on correlative evidence and require functional validation before causal conclusions can be drawn. This review synthesizes current knowledge on the molecular mechanisms by which SLC25A39 integrates mGSH transport with iron metabolism, and critically evaluates its emerging roles across different cancer types. We propose that beyond serving as a candidate prognostic biomarker, SLC25A39 represents a potential therapeutic target whose clinical utility remains to be established, and we discuss key unanswered questions regarding its tissue-specific functions and the translational challenges that lie ahead.

title: Cancer-associated fibroblasts and immune evasion in endometrial cancer: current evidence and therapeutic perspectives.
abstract: Cancer-associated fibroblasts (CAFs) are potential contributors to tumor progression and immune resistance in endometrial cancer (EC), but the extent of EC-specific mechanistic and therapeutic evidence remains uneven. Studies using EC-derived fibroblasts support tumor-promoting paracrine activity and provide experimental evidence of altered natural killer cell function. Single-cell and spatial analyses further characterize stromal heterogeneity and candidate intercellular interactions. However, many proposed mechanisms of CAF-mediated immune exclusion and most CAF-directed therapeutic strategies are informed by studies in other malignancies. This review distinguishes findings obtained in EC patient samples and experimental models from evidence extrapolated from pancreatic, breast, gastric, and other cancers. We examine CAF heterogeneity, soluble signaling, matrix remodeling, and immune-cell interactions, while identifying where functional validation in EC is still required. Therapeutic approaches, including FAP-directed interventions, stromal reprogramming, and signaling blockade combined with immune checkpoint inhibition, are discussed as candidate research strategies rather than established EC treatments. Priorities include validating CAF-immune mechanisms in EC, developing reproducible stromal biomarkers, and testing treatment combinations in appropriate disease-specific models and clinical studies.

title: Online Information-Seeking Behaviour for Major Cancers: A 10-Year Infodemiological Study to Inform Public Health and Health Promotion Priorities in Hungary.
abstract: Background/Objectives: To analyse trends in online information-seeking behaviour for five major cancers in Hungary, compare them with global trends, and assess changes during the COVID-19 pandemic, cancer-related awareness campaigns, and major cancer-related events on search activity. Methods: A retrospective observational infodemiological study was conducted using Google Trends™ (GT) data for lung, colorectal, breast, prostate, and pancreatic cancers between 2013 and 2022. Search intensity was assessed using uncorrected relative search volume (RSVraw) as the primary measure, complemented by RSVsens, as an Internet penetration-adjusted sensitivity analysis. Descriptive statistics, parametric tests, time-series and seasonality analyses, Mann-Kendall tests, and joinpoint regression were performed using IBM SPSS Statistics 22.0, PAST 4.03, and Joinpoint 5.3.0 (α: 0.05; 95% confidence interval [CI]). Benjamini-Hochberg (BH) false discovery rate (FDR) correction was applied for multiple testing.
